#1077. Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."

#1074. Chelsea Confidential: Meet Sebas Parrilla, the fiery, marathon-running, Bruce Springsteen fan Xabi Alonso trusts above all others - and why he's the man to fix Blues' defensive crisis

Published: 12:00 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 12:04 EST, 25 November 2026

Xabi Alonso is not alone in trying to halt Chelsea’s lurch into crisis. He is surrounded by a small army of staff. Some may be familiar to you, others less so.

There is Willie Isa, the ‘cultural architect’ preparing the defenders for headed duels by acting as a human shield in training drills.

There is Andre Reis, the new set-piece analyst studying Nottingham Forest’s approach to corners so Austin MacPhee can formulate instructions for the team.

There is Simon Morris and Stu Sullivan, the sports massage therapists preparing the players for their Friday night turnaround. And so on.

But the voice Alonso trusts most at Chelsea belongs to Sebastian Parrilla Simione, better known as ‘Sebas’.

The little-known Argentinian, a 49-year-old with a UEFA Pro Licence and love of marathon running and Bruce Springsteen, is his closest confidant and has been by his side ever since they oversaw an unbeaten season for Real Madrid’s Under 14s in 2018-19.

Xabi Alonso's most trusted lieutenant is Sebastian 'Sebas' Parrilla, a 49-year-old Bruce Springsteen fan with a tendency to get fired up on the touchline

Alonso had asked for an experienced aide to assist him at Real, and he was handed Parrilla, who was born in Argentina, raised in Spain, and despite not playing professionally had worked for Madrid’s academy since 2002. Parrilla coached all age ranges, from the Under 11s to the B team.

He had Alonso’s ear as their Under 14s won all but one game, and their bond was strong enough that Parrilla ended his 17-year association with Madrid’s academy when he accompanied his manager to Real Sociedad B in 2019. Then he followed him to Bayer Leverkusen in 2022, back to Real Madrid in 2025, and now Chelsea.

There is a little fire to Parrilla. He is already one caution away from a touchline suspension, having been booked against Tottenham Hotspur and Everton. While the analytical Parrilla prefers a low profile, he is Alonso’s alter ego.

The English winter will not only test Parrilla’s preference for wearing shorts whatever the weather, but also Chelsea's ability to arrest their slump with games coming thick and fast – there are seven Premier League fixtures to tackle between now and 2027, starting with Forest on Friday.

One area of focus on the training field this week has been defence. Chelsea have conceded 20 goals in the Premier League, as many as they have scored. Their shakiness at the back has been their downfall of late, and Parrilla was credited with helping organise the Leverkusen back line which went unbeaten in winning the Bundesliga in 2023-24.

When Leverkusen won 5-1 away at Eintracht Frankfurt in May 2024 to maintain their Invincibles tag with two games to go, Alonso was serving a touchline ban. Parrilla manned the technical area and after full time, Granit Xhaka and Co celebrated by pouring water over him.

Parrilla was fine with that, but less pleased during the game with how they conceded a goal from a corner to Hugo Ekitike and gifted other chances to Omar Marmoush.

One source at Leverkusen that we consulted this week credited Parrilla with improving players individually and taking the lead on set-pieces.

When Leverkusen scored from one corner routine against Hoffenheim in November 2023, Parrilla was the architect. He had certain players act as barriers to stop defenders from rushing to block the ball as it was rolled to the edge of the box, where Alex Grimaldo was on hand to power home.

Chelsea have their own set-piece specialist in MacPhee, poached from Aston Villa in the summer, so Parrilla has less control over set-pieces at Cobham.

We do not yet know whether Alonso and Parrilla will decide to change Chelsea’s centre backs for Forest. Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana were bullied by Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey and Leeds United’s Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the last two losses.

Former Chelsea man Liam Delap is the next No9 to contend with, and won't be short on motivation.

There is the added complication that Fofana has conducted an unauthorised interview, released this week, in which he laughed off Chelsea's Carabao Cup exit after his penalty miss at Liverpool. Chelsea declined to comment when asked whether that would lead to any internal punishment.

Alonso and Parrilla have been joined at the hip since the former began working with Real Madrid's Under 14s in 2018

Levi Colwill was bullied by Leeds' Dominic Calvert-Lewin in Chelsea's humiliating 4-1 loss last weekend

Alonso’s options are limited. Frustrated as he will have been by his side's 4-1 loss to Leeds, he had no senior replacements for Colwill or Fofana to call on from the bench. The only substitute with 'experience' at centre back was 18-year-old Olutayo Subuloye.

Aaron Anselmino, who represented Argentina in the last international break but has not appeared for Chelsea at all this season, did not make the matchday squad.

Maxence Lacroix is still sidelined, but Alonso told us last week he hopes he will return before 2027. Josh Acheampong and Jorrel Hato could be used centrally rather than as full backs.

As well as assisting Alonso, Parrilla acted as a bridge to the academy at Leverkusen, regularly in contact with Sergi Runge when he was head coach of the Under 17s and Under 19s.

Despite the success of the first team, Parrilla never lost the love for coaching youngsters, agreeing to help the Under 8s with community sessions on occasion. Throwing in Subuloye, who was on Chelsea’s pre-season tour in the summer but has yet to appear competitively, would surely be too big of an ask.

Until better options arrive, it would seem Parrilla is having to try to work his magic in the shadows with Colwill and Fofana. Both players know they need to improve – and fast.

Mamadou Sarr is with Real Sociedad, a loan which is also believed not to contain an option to buy, but the 21-year-old has been starting regularly for them in La Liga and the Europa League.

Other loans include Dastan Satpayev, the 18-year-old Kazakh who has been given a harsh welcome to English football with Championship strugglers Burnley (and is also injured), and Caleb Wiley, 21, also in the relegation zone with Preston.

#1068. Celtic's European opponents are plankton in football's great ocean... but Portuguese second-tier strugglers Torreense have already made waves in Europe this season

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 12:29 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 12:33 EST, 25 November 2026

Even for aficionados of the continental game, the draw for the Europa League this year was likely to cause a degree of puzzlement.

While not the only outfit to be making its debut in one of UEFA’s competitions, the name of S.C.U. Torreense rang precious few bells among supporters of clubs with a vested interest in how the cards might fall. And little wonder.

The Portuguese side are plankton in football’s great ocean. Not only have they never played on this stage before, they haven’t even come close to it.

An extraordinary triumph in the Portuguese Cup final – the Taca de Portugal – against Sporting Lisbon in May was their ticket to this journey. In all likelihood, this European adventure will be their first and their last.

It is, of course, not the done thing for anyone connected with any particular club to express a preference as to who they might be drawn against. But representatives of any one of the 35 other sides present at the Grimaldi Forum in Monaco in late August who claimed they weren’t privately hoping for a match against the men from the small city of Torres Vedras were lying.

Never mind Benfica, Porto and Sporting Lisbon, the traditional footballing powerhouses of that nation. In terms of support, stature and history, this outfit are a world removed from the likes of Braga and Vitoria Guimaraes, the perennial challengers to the big three.

Torreense players celebrate their victory over Armenian side Ararat in their last European tie

Torreense’s place in the food chain is underscored by the fact that they can’t even play European matches in their 2,400-capacity Estadio Manuel Marques home because it doesn’t match UEFA criteria.

For the purposes of the Europa League, their fans, who primarily hail from a place which sits 25 miles north of Lisbon, will have to travel to Leiria, which is 60 miles north of their home.

Those looking to pick up a late ticket for the visit of Celtic should have no concerns. Built for Euro 2004, the Estadio Municipal de Leiria holds 23,888 spectators. Torreense, who were a tier three side as recently as 2022, draw an average crowd of around 1,300.

The fact is that it’s not only a second division Portuguese side which Martin O’Neill’s men will face on matchday five. It’s a struggling one.

After ten matches in Liga Portugal 2, Joao Nuno’s men lie 13th of 18, 31st place overall in Portugal. They’ve won just twice this season, against Amarante and Benfica B, and have already had their cup defence ended by Benfica’s big boys.

Nuno was only appointed at the end of October after Luis Tralhao, who lifted the only major honour in the club’s history, was fired after a dismal start.

Portuguese coach Joao Nuno only took charge at the struggling second-tier side this season

Yet the concern for O’Neill and his players is that the Torreense which routinely fails to impress in its domestic division bears little resemblance to the one which has so far pitched up on its maiden European adventure.

In one of the most eye-catching results of the opening night, the Portuguese minnows travelled to Norway and defeated Lillestrom, a respected name throughout Europe, 2-1.

Sunderland were the first visitors to Leiria in October. What a game Torreense gave the Premier League side, leading by a goal only to narrowly lose the match late on.

While a 4-1 loss to Celtic’s old foes Ferencvaros in Budapest was something of a reality check, Nuno’s players fought back from a goal down to beat Ararat-Armenia in injury time last time out at their adopted home.

So, despite being wretched in their own league, they have six points in the Europa League and presently sit in 19th place, above the likes of Real Sociedad, AC Milan and Marseille.

With nine points possibly being enough to squeeze through to the play-off round, a famous win against Celtic could do the trick with three games to spare. With around £400,000 earned in prize money for any victory, you’d better believe they’ll be up for this.

Having just about lived to tell the tale last month, Sunderland boss Regis Le Bris gave Celtic a warning about what lies in store on Thursday.

Despite their lowly status, Torreense are above AC Milan, Celtic and Marseille in the table

‘It’s a good team they know how to manage this kind of game,’ said the Frenchman. ‘They’re well organised and hard to break down with this deep block. They try to seize every opportunity.’

A limited side which sits in and plays with caution? Those Celtic supporters who had the misfortune to watch their favourites fail to break down an atrocious Kairat Almaty outfit across 210 minutes little over a year ago will be rightly concerned.

While the Parkhead men’s poor record on the road across many years includes some thumpings at the hands of super clubs including Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain, there have been enough stumbles against lesser sides to ensure nothing can be taken for granted.

O’Neill will point to the displays in last season’s victories away to Feyenoord and Stuttgart as examples of what he’s looking for. While not on his watch, the catastrophe away to Kairat remains a useful illustration of what may happen if the players aren’t at it.

With an early goal likely to kick the legs from under Torreense, Celtic cannot allow them to feel comfortable in their shape.

In order to disrupt the Portuguese, it will be a night for the visitors to play with speed and imagination. To get in behind their defence, O’Neill’s wingers need to shine.

Sunderland required a late goal from Noah Sadiki to emerge with a victory on their trip to Leiria

This will have informed the veteran’s thinking as he sought to draft in a replacement for the injured Mika Baur.

While bringing in Joel van den Berg would have made sense from a positional point of view, Jota has started to show signs that he’s moving through the levels after a year-and-a-half out injured. A goal or an assist on his return to his homeland would allow the former Benfica man to underscore that point.

A constant threat against St Mirren, Yang Hyun-jun should start on the right flank ahead of Haissem Hassan. Together with Seb Tounekti, the Egyptian increasingly feels like a peripheral player.

Even if Benjamin Nygren is available again after a heel injury, O’Neill will be loath to drop Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain or Luke McCowan after both showed up well when played alongside Callum McGregor in the weekend win.

The issue of Kasper Hogh’s 16-game goal drought will only become pertinent if the free-scoring Camilo Duran can first help to put the game to bed.

Fit-again winger Jota could feature for Celtic on his return to Portuguese soil

Celtic badly need this to be a rare straightforward evening on the road in Europe. Goodness knows, they’ve had precious few of those in recent times.

A win to go with the one they claimed last time out against Besiktas would leave them in a decent position in the competition, with a further four points from their remaining matches with Omonia, Marseille and Union Saint-Gilloise then assuring them of progression.

Anything other than that outcome tonight doesn’t bear thinking about. Almost 60 years on from Jock Stein’s side becoming sporting immortals by defeating Inter Milan in Lisbon, their successors must tick a box and ensure tiny Torreense’s reputation in the game remains as lowly as it has ever been.

Honking weather here in Barcelona with the rain hammering down at the Nou Camp.

No such luck, however, and it is pretty torrential at the moment. Football updates to follow.

Aston Villa have made the trip over to Spain to take on Barcelona in the Champions League on matchday four. These teams last met all the way back in 1983, when they met in the European Super Cup. Barcelona won the first leg 1-0 at home before Aston Villa claimed a 3-0 victory at Villa Park, meaning Villa progressed 3-1 on aggregate.

Aston Villa have made the perfect start to their Champions League campaign, winning all three games, beating Club Brugge, Fenerbahce and Viking, scoring 12 goals in the process. Unai Emery’s side drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday. Emery, who celebrates his 55th birthday today, has a very dismal record against Barcelona, taking just three wins from 30 matches. His last Champions League game at the Nou Camp was infamous as his PSG side lost 6-1 to go out in the last 16 back in 2017 despite winning the first leg of that tie 4-0.

“In 1982, Villa won the European Cup, and we like to think about playing in this competition again and trying to repeat that success,” Emery said. “Barcelona are favourites for what they have done in the last ten years; now they need to prove why they are favourites.

“[Barcelona] have [Lamine] Yamal. He is a special player. You can see in him as a player who could end up being the best. He needs a few things but he could end up being a great player. Rodri gives personality to the team. They have [Anthony] Gordon giving them speed and hard work. They have Pedri or Fermin [Lopez] as offensive midfielders.”

Barcelona started strongly in the Champions League, winning their first two games, but lost 4-2 at defending champions PSG last time out. They warmed up for this match with an emphatic 6-1 win over Alaves in La Liga on Saturday. That victory gives them a two-point lead at the summit of La Liga.

“We know that at this level, anything can happen,” Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said. “Against Real Madrid, the result could have been different. These are special matches, but we are staying confident. It is normal to focus more on our last two defeats, but I have confidence in my team, which showed it again on Saturday. Now, we are focused on the Champions League, with the goal of finishing in the top eight. For me, he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world and he has reaped extraordinary successes. His team’s style of play is clear and very well organised. Just look at how they execute set pieces; it is something impressive. Their confidence in themselves is unmatched. It will be a tough match against a great team and a great coach.”

Team news from Nou Camp to follow shortly.

#1065. LA communities kick out Big Oil

After years of advocacy from residents and legal battles with Big Oil, Los Angeles voted to ban drilling and phase out oil extraction in the city. It's the first city in the United States to kick the oil industry out.

Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells .

"Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," said local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans the redrilling or deepening of wells. Existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.

Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

"In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," said council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site."

Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property."

LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.

California's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

Today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.

Under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," said Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.

Miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.

LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.

California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman said energy companies were prepared to challenge the new ordinance.

Zierman added that it would make city residents more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.

"It sends the jobs, investment and revenue elsewhere while leaving Californians to pay the bill," said Zierman.

The relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

Even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

California's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the coastal lowlands known as the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.

When wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA fire department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.

But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

The cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging plans or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.

But those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million (€32 million) in fines in 2025.

A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup."  For now, she is says both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air."

#1064. Single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map for coronary artery disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Although coronary artery disease (CAD) genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci, most variants lie in non-coding regions, obscuring the causal gene programmes and cell types driving disease1,2. Here we performed single-nucleus multi-omic profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility in human coronary arteries from 44 people to construct a genome-wide single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map. We identified 11,269 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) across principal vascular cell types, including CAD-associated caQTLs in smooth muscle cells (SMCs). Using dynamic single-cell caQTL modelling3, we show that variant effects on chromatin vary across SMC states. For example, rs658956-mediated suppression of the FGGY-DT enhancer through disruption of an AP-1 motif is amplified as SMCs transition towards a fibromyocyte fate. We next performed genome-wide high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) in 15 human coronary arteries, showing that rs4887091 in the ADAMTS7 CAD locus has allele-dependent effects on CCCTC-binding factor occupancy and loop strength. Integrating Hi-C, Hi-C with chromatin immunoprecipitation and in vitro clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats interference (CRISPRi) nominated AMOTL2 as a distal SMC-specific CAD gene whose loss promotes proliferation and suppresses contractile identity. Finally, arrayed Perturb–seq of GWAS-nominated enhancers converged on extracellular matrix remodelling as a core SMC disease programme. Together, these findings provide a framework for mapping non-coding GWAS variants to cell types, chromatin states and gene programmes in human disease.

Common diseases are driven by a multitude of factors and remain difficult to treat given the lack of a unified disease mechanism4. Coronary artery disease (CAD) is among the most prevalent common chronic diseases, and numerous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have now identified hundreds of variants linked to CAD risk. Although these results may potentially pave the way for new therapeutic target discovery1,2,5,6, much of the translation from GWAS to therapeutic targets for CAD has been restricted to lipid-lowering drugs7,8. Large-scale clinical studies have demonstrated a persistent residual risk of CAD independent of lipid levels9,10, but we lack drugs that directly target disease pathways in the vessel wall due to an incomplete understanding of causal disease mechanisms. Leveraging human genetics to uncover new lipid-independent biological mechanisms and drug targets in CAD represents a tremendous unmet need and would be a principal milestone in translating population-scale GWAS findings to therapies for patients11,12.

Although population-scale GWAS offer great opportunity for target discovery, most identified variants lie within non-coding regions of the genome, making it difficult to dissect the causal cell types and molecular pathways13. The advent of single-cell sequencing technologies now allows for the profiling of human tissues in health and disease at unprecedented granularity14. Previous studies have used traditional single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) for detailed characterization of cell states in human tissue that drive disease15,16,17,18; however, these studies do not profile the non-coding genome, making it challenging to link GWAS variants to observed molecular changes. More recently, single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC) with sequencing (snATAC–seq) in human coronary arteries was conducted to link CAD GWAS variants to regulatory elements19. Although this represented an important advance in the field, the lack of complementary transcriptomic profiling rendered it challenging to nominate causal genes in vascular cell types. Furthermore, isolated snATAC–seq precludes the discovery of distal gene regulation as a driver of disease20, and there are currently no studies that profile the three-dimensional (3D) chromatin architecture in human coronary arteries to enable the investigation of these distal regulatory connections.

Herein we performed simultaneous multi-omic profiling of the transcriptome and epigenome in nuclei from 44 human coronary arteries to build a multi-omic enhancer–gene map of CAD. Collectively, these analyses identified CAD-associated regulatory variants and enhancer–gene links in smooth muscle cells (SMCs), motivating focused analysis of SMC state-dependent gene regulation. To expand insight into gene regulation across functionally heterogeneous SMC cell states, we used dynamic chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTL) modelling to uncover cell-state-dependent pathogenicity of disease variants. To dissect the role of disease-associated variants in regulating larger scale gene networks, we performed genome-wide Hi-C in 15 human coronary arteries to link variants to distal genes and validated our findings using cell-specific high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) with chromatin immunoprecipitation (Hi-ChIP–seq) and in vitro CRISPRi. Finally, we performed Perturb–seq in human coronary artery SMCs (HCASMCs) to characterize functional mechanisms of repressing disease-associated enhancers and genes. Collectively, we provide a multi-omic map of human CAD by integrating transcriptomic, epigenetic and chromatin architecture to link disease-associated genetic variants with candidate disease-relevant cell types and target genes.

We performed single-nucleus Multi-ome (RNA+ATAC) sequencing in 44 human coronary arteries from non-failing donors and patients with chronic heart failure isolated at the time of heart transplantation (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). After quality control, we recovered 126,804 nuclei from 11 distinct cell types (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Fig. 1b–d). Using differential expression of canonical genes, we identified clusters corresponding to all main vascular cell types, including coronary artery SMCs (MYH11, ACTA2, ITGA8), endothelial cells (VWF, LDB2, PECAM1), fibroblasts (LAMA2, DCN, FBLN1) and myeloid cells (F13A1, CD163, MRC1) (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1a–c and Supplementary Table 2). We used MACS2 to identify areas of open chromatin (‘peaks’) from the ATAC–seq data (Fig. 1e) and identified 143,743 cell-type-specific differentially accessible peaks (Extended Data Fig. 1d,e). Generally, cell-type clustering was concordant between the RNA and ATAC data. However, gene-expression data enabled the annotation of rarer cell types that were not captured by ATAC-based clustering alone (Supplementary Fig. 1e–g). Using differentially accessible peaks across cells, we also discovered cell-type-specific enrichment of transcriptional motifs such as SpiB and PU.1 in myeloid cells, MEF2B/C/D in SMCs and CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein in adipocytes (Supplementary Fig. 1h). We linked peaks to genes using a new supervised single-cell model called single-cell enhancer-to-gene (E2G) (scE2G)21 (Fig. 1d, Extended Data Fig. 2a–g and Supplementary Tables 3–14; Methods). We found that the non-immune cells had the greatest number of shared enhancers relative to myeloid cells (Fig. 1d) and that all cell types had a similar number of E2G links (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 3).

a, Study design. b, Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embedding plot of integrated data clustered by RNA. c, Cell-type composition stack plot by sample. NK, natural killer. d, Number of shared enhancers heatmap (right) from scE2G map (left); defined as the number of enhancers where more than 50% of the peak width overlaps with other cell type-specific peaks. e, Number of scE2G links in the main cell types. f, Linkage disequilibrium score regression (LDSC) for cardiometabolic traits by cell type; dotted line, multiple-testing-adjusted P value threshold. P values were calculated using one-sided stratified LDSC, with Bonferroni correction for six conditions (P < 8.33 × 10−3). Illustrations in a and d created in BioRender: a, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/ib7ak3x (2026); d, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/cwi31gk (2026).

Notably, we found that cardiometabolic disease variants for CAD, systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) were enriched in differentially accessible marker peaks specific to SMCs and endothelial cells (Fig. 1f). As a predominantly non-vascular trait, diabetes did not demonstrate enrichment of disease-associated variants (Fig. 1f).

To boost our power for single-cell caQTL (sc-caQTL) discovery, we integrated our Multi-ome ATAC–seq data with available snATAC–seq data from human coronary arteries19 to create a meta-map of 88 samples and 245,562 nuclei across four ancestry groups (Extended Data Fig. 3a–f). We then used RASQUAL to identify pseudobulk caQTLs in four principal vascular cell types (SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells, fibroblasts) (Fig. 2a). At the 10% false discovery rate (FDR) threshold, we found 11,269 significant caQTL associations in SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells and fibroblasts (Extended Data Fig. 3g–i, Supplementary Fig. 2a–d and Supplementary Tables 15–26). Power, sensitivity, subsampling and runtime analyses are shown in Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3 and described in Supplementary Methods.

a, Schematic of sc-caQTL discovery with disease enrichment. b, Number of sc-caQTLs by cell type at FDR 0.05. c, Regional Manhattan plot of CAD GWAS1 and SMC caQTL results at the rs658956 locus. d, snATAC–seq tracks with E2G link centred at the rs658956 locus showing SMC-specific enrichment of the enhancer with an E2G link to FGGY-DT. e, Violin plot showing normalized expression by genotype for rs658956 and FGGY-DT in coronary arteries from GTEx (P = 3.39 × 10−12). The P value was calculated using a two-sided t-test of the GTEx eQTL linear regression coefficient against zero. f, PRINT and seq2PRINT transcription factor binding prediction pipeline (left). rs658956 overlaps region with high transcription factor binding probability from seq2PRINT model (top) and multiscale footprinting associates rs658956 with a transcription factor-specific footprint (bottom). g, Motif analysis finds rs658956 overlaps canonical AP-1 transcription factor (JUN, FOS) motifs. Ref, reference alelle; Alt, alternate allele. h, EMSA demonstrates a binding shift in the reference allele sequence (containing G) that was not present in the alternative allele sequence (containing T) when these allelic sequences were exposed to nuclear lysate from SMCs (n = 3 replicates, representative experiment shown). i, Dynamic caQTL modelling and discovery strategy (cell-state-dependent). j, rs658956 caQTL dynamic effect size. Net effect size depicted here represents the sum of \({\beta }_{g}\) and \({\beta }_{{\rm{F}}{\rm{M}}{\rm{C}}{\rm{x}}{\rm{G}}}\) in our generalized linear mixed model across cells. k, rs658956 genotype association with normalized chromatin accessibility across FMC tertiles. Negative slope of association increases as FMC score increases; n = 268 (e) and n = 79 (k) biologically independent samples were used. Illustrations in a and i created in BioRender: a, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/cwi31gk (2026); i, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/m3r2gap (2026).

We further characterized caQTL variants to assess their regulatory potential. Lead caQTL variants were enriched strongly near the peaks they were predicted to regulate, consistent with a cis-regulatory mechanism (Extended Data Fig. 3j). We next overlapped our pseudobulk caQTLs and GTEx bulk arterial tissue eQTLs by cell type and found several hundred shared QTL variants in SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells and fibroblasts (Extended Data Fig. 3i). Furthermore, we found a strong correlation in effect size between our SMC caQTLs and bulk coronary artery eQTLs from GTEx (Extended Data Fig. 3k). Finally, in SMCs we trained a convolutional neural net model (seq2PRINT22) that incorporates chromatin accessibility and ATAC footprinting to predict transcription factor binding probability at a base-pair resolution. We found that caQTL variants within accessible peaks had significantly higher predicted transcription factor binding probabilities compared with all other non-caQTL SNP sites within accessible peaks (P = 8.2 × 10−40, Wilcoxon rank sum) (Extended Data Fig. 3l).

To identify disease-associated caQTLs, we overlapped sc-caQTLs for each cell type with CAD GWAS variants (defined as lead variants associated with CAD at 1% FDR1 and variants in linkage disequilibrium with these at R2 ≥ 0.8 in the European population from 1000 Genomes Project; Supplementary Table 27), which yielded numerous disease-relevant cell-type-specific caQTLs (Extended Data Fig. 3m). For example, we found that rs7182567 was an SMC-specific caQTL that was also a GWAS variant (P = 5.4 × 10−26) and a bulk GTEx eQTL for ADAMTS7 in tibial artery (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Similarly, we found that rs8017642 is an endothelial cell-specific caQTL in the NEK9 locus (Extended Data Fig. 4b), whereas rs2337154 and rs1443120 are fibroblast- and myeloid-specific caQTLs, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d).

Next, we leveraged the paired RNA data to sub-cluster SMCs into transcriptionally distinct cell states, forming a continuum from ‘healthy’ contractile SMC states (SMC1–3) to de-differentiated ‘disease-associated’ SMC states including fibromyocytes (FMCs) and chondromyocytes (CMCs) (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Notably, we found that ADAMTS7 was expressed most highly in FMCs (Extended Data Fig. 4e), indicating a role in disease regulation. To identify functionally distinct endothelial cell states, we mapped our data to a high-resolution scRNA-seq atherosclerosis atlas23 and identified four transcriptionally distinct endothelial subsets (Extended Data Fig. 4f). Notably, NEK9 was expressed in endothelial cells enriched with endothelium-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) genes such as COL1A1 and FN1 (refs. 24,25) (Extended Data Fig. 4f,g). Pathway enrichment in the EMT population showed increased EMT and stress-response signals (Extended Data Fig. 4h). Next, we created a gene set score comprised of 41 endothelial cell-specific genes thought to be associated causally with CAD26 that showed maximal enrichment in intimal endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 4i). Similarly, we created a gene signature of a gene programme26 identified previously as driving CAD pathogenesis in endothelial cells (Programme 8) and found an enrichment of this programme in angiogenic and/or vasa vasorum endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 4j).

The CAD disease-associated variant rs658956 illustrates how a cell-type-specific caQTL can impart functional transcriptional changes. The variant is an SMC-specific and fibroblast-specific caQTL and regulates a putative enhancer element (chr. 1: 59169569–59170069), which is linked to the gene FGGY-DT in an SMC-specific manner by scE2G (Fig. 2c,d). Consistently, we found that rs658956 is also a coronary artery eQTL for FGGY-DT expression (P = 3.4 × 10−12) wherein the alternative allele (T) is associated with decreased expression relative to the reference allele (G) (Fig. 2e) and is also predicted to overlie a high probability transcription factor binding site (Fig. 2f). Motif-based transcription factor binding site analysis found that rs658956 is predicted to disrupt a core AP-1 (JUN/FOS) transcription factor binding motif (5′-TGAGTCA-3′) (Fig. 2g). Electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) demonstrated a binding shift in the reference allele sequence (containing G) that was not present in the alternative allele sequence (containing T) when these alleles were exposed to nuclear lysate from SMCs (Fig. 2h). Antibody supershift EMSA confirmed that the shifted AP-1 complex band consists of JUN and FOS transcription factors (Extended Data Fig. 4k). Together, these results suggest that the disease-associated variant rs658956 impacts transcription factor binding, thereby decreasing the chromatin accessibility of the enhancer and subsequently reducing FGGY-DT expression in a SMC-specific manner.

In atherosclerosis, SMCs undergo a well-characterized phenotypic switch from a contractile state to a fibroblast-like FMC phenotype16, driven by disease-associated transcriptional programmes. To characterize this transition, individual nuclei were assigned an FMC score based on FMC state marker genes for downstream modelling (Fig. 2i and Extended Data Fig. 5a–d). Notably, this FMC gene score is dynamic with disease across species, disease burden, pseudotime trajectory, in vitro HCASMC stress and transcriptional regulation (Extended Data Fig. 5e–k). To identify state-dependent caQTL effects, we used a Poisson mixed-effects (PME) single-cell model (Extended Data Fig. 6a–c; Methods). Applying this PME model to the lead variants of SMC-specific pseudobulk caQTLs, we identified 712 caQTLs whose effects were dynamic with respect to the FMC score (FDR ≤ 5%) (Supplementary Tables 29 and 30). Notably, eight of these dynamic caQTLs were also disease-associated variants. For example, rs658956 exhibited a significant interaction with FMC score (FDR-adjusted likelihood ratio test (LRT) P value = 2.36 × 10−4) (Fig. 2j,k). A negative interaction term indicates that, as the FMC score increased, the negative association between rs658956 and local chromatin accessibility was amplified (Fig. 2j,k). Using the scE2G map to link dynamic caQTL-related enhancer elements (caPeaks) to target genes, we found that extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling was the most enriched pathway among linked genes (Extended Data Fig. 6d,e and Supplementary Table 31). Notably, several of these genes linked to dynamic caPeaks were enriched in FMCs (Extended Data Fig. 6f and Supplementary Table 32). Similar state-dependent effects were observed at other CAD loci such as dynamic caQTL variant rs11838776 in the COL4A1 locus, suggesting that COL4A1 may play a role during transition toward an FMC state (Extended Data Fig. 6g–k). Collectively, these dynamic analyses demonstrate that disease-associated variants can exert cell-state-dependent regulatory effects on chromatin accessibility.

To map CAD disease-associated variants to cell types and genes in an unbiased fashion, we built a disease-relevant single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map (scV2E2G) integrating cell-type-specific regulatory elements, CAD GWAS variants, scE2G links and caQTLs21,27 (Fig. 3a; Methods).

Overlapping scE2G with sc-caQTLs provides a high-fidelity set of predicted variants that may be driving disease by directly regulating intermediate molecular traits in a cell-type-specific manner.

Focusing on the 325 genes linked to SMC enhancers harbouring CAD GWAS variants, we performed several enrichment analyses. These analyses found that these linked genes were over-represented in nearest lead genes from CAD and myocardial infarction GWAS, identified GATA2 as the most enriched transcription factor and highlighted collagen and ECM remodelling as key biological processes (Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Tables 37–39). Correlation analysis between gene expression and FMC score identified FN1, COL4A1, COL4A2, MFGE8 and MYO9B—all known CAD-associated genes implicated in ECM remodelling—among the most highly correlated transcripts (Extended Data Fig. 7b and Supplementary Table 40). Notably, the enhancer harbouring variant rs7246865 emerged as potentially important in disease, acting as both a cell-state dynamic caPeak and pseudobulk caPeak in SMCs with a high-confidence scE2G link (Fig. 3b). We confirmed this predicted link experimentally using CRISPRi in HCASMCs. Repressing the rs7246865-containing enhancer significantly reduced MYO9B expression relative to a non-targeting control (Fig. 3c), consistent with previous functional validation at this locus1. Furthermore, CRISPRi validated scE2G predictions in SMCs for three additional loci near genes LOXL1, NAV1 and PALLD; enhancer repression altered gene expression significantly at each of these loci relative to non-targeting controls (Extended Data Fig. 7c–e).

To further validate scE2G links, we performed arrayed CRISPRi Perturb–seq in HCASMCs, delivering individual sgRNAs to target either the transcription start site (TSS) or the nominated enhancer at eight CAD GWAS loci (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 41). Alongside transcriptional profiling, we measured SMC proliferation by live-cell imaging, revealing that several perturbations (including ADAMTS7, CFDP1 and COL4A1) and significantly reduced proliferation rate, with enhancer knockdowns generally phenocopying their cognate TSS perturbations (Fig. 3e, Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Table 42). Following quality control, we retained 76,179 cells and confirmed robust, perturbation-specific transcriptional responses, with selective target-gene knockdown, stronger effects for TSS than enhancer perturbations and separation from non-targeting controls (Extended Data Fig. 8b–j).

Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed locus-specific pathway enrichments: BMP1 and ADAMTS7 knockdowns strongly enriched MYC and E2F target-gene sets, whereas CFDP1 and COL4A1 knockdowns suppressed interferon response pathways, indicating distinct downstream transcriptional consequences across CAD loci (Extended Data Fig. 9a). Consensus non-negative matrix factorization identified six biologically interpretable programmes: inflammation, ECM remodelling, vascular remodelling, interferon response and two proliferative programmes corresponding to S and M phase (Extended Data Fig. 9b,c and Supplementary Tables 43 and 44). Notably, the ECM remodelling programme showed the strongest positive correlation with the FMC module score, with enhancer knockdowns of CFDP1, MYO9B and BMP1 exhibiting the highest mean FMC scores (Extended Data Fig. 9d–h). Programme-level analysis further revealed that COL4A1 and its enhancer were the strongest drivers of the inflammation programme, whereas the MRAS and CFDP1 enhancer perturbations modulated both inflammation and ECM remodelling (Fig. 3f).

Finally, robust rank aggregation (RRA) across pseudobulk DESeq2 profiles revealed a convergent gene programme dominated by downregulation of several collagen genes (COL3A1, COL4A1, COL5A1, COL6A1–A3) and TIMP2, alongside the upregulation of metabolic and stress-response genes (Fig. 3g, Extended Data Fig. 9i and Supplementary Table 45). Pathway enrichment of this convergent programme identified EMT, tumour necrosis factor signalling through nuclear factor κB, and mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 signalling as the top enriched terms (Fig. 3h). Collectively, these findings implicate a shared regulatory framework that governs SMC phenotypic states across independent, disease-associated loci.

To investigate how disease-associated variants may influence broader gene networks through chromatin looping, we performed genome-wide Hi-C in 15 human coronary arteries to construct large-scale chromatin networks (Fig. 4a, Extended Data Fig. 10a–f and Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6). To further complement Hi-C in bulk tissue, we performed H3K27Ac Hi-ChIP–seq in cultured human coronary artery smooth muscle cells and endothelial cells. Comparing the number of enhancer–gene connection overlap by method, we found that scE2GMulti-ome and Hi-ChIP yielded the highest number of enhancer–gene connections, with a smaller fraction from bulk coronary tissue Hi-C (Supplementary Fig. 7). We then identified groups of genomic loci that interact preferentially with one another in specific chromatin networks termed ‘mosaics’ (Fig. 4a; Methods). We identified 5,130 mosaics containing 11,494 protein-coding genes. Notably, mosaics harbouring a disease-associated variant exhibited significantly higher structural complexity, containing an average of 25 loops compared with 14 loops in non-disease-associated mosaics (P = 1.7 × 10−17) (Fig. 4b). This approach provides a framework for mapping disease-associated variants to a catalogue of genes regulated distally through interconnected chromatin networks (Supplementary Tables 46–49).

The enlarged area shows loop contact coloured by inherent score. e, Inherent score of the boundary loop from d in all samples grouped by genotypes at rs4887091, where each bar represents a single person. f, Allele-specific loops from phased genotype framework (left) and boundary loop inherent score resolved from phased genotypes showing increased looping strength in the reference allele (C) at rs4887091. Next, we performed CTCF ChIP–seq in HCASMC to prioritize disease-associated SMC enhancers that are bound by CTCF. Of all CAD disease-associated variants, 498 overlapped CTCF peaks, including 200 within accessible chromatin regions. CAD-associated variants were enriched significantly at CTCF-bound regions above permutation-based expectation (1.25-fold, P = 0.02; Extended Data Fig. 10g).

Among the top-ranking regulatory mosaics, we identified mosaic-1664, which contains the CAD-associated variant rs4887091 located within an SMC enhancer (Fig. 4c). In this mosaic, we found an 800-kb boundary loop exhibiting a strong rs4887091 genotype-dependent increase in contact strength for the alternate allele (C) relative to the reference allele (T) (Fig. 4d). Specifically, the loop strength increased in a dose-dependent manner when quantified across all samples, where there was minimal contact strength in homozygotes (T|T), moderate strength in heterozygotes (T|C, C|T) and highest strength in homozygotes (C|C) (Fig. 4e). Phased genotypes confirmed increased looping strength on the C allele (P = 3.1 × 10−3) (Fig. 4f).

To characterize the regulatory architecture of rs4887091 within mosaic-1664, we identified all genes linked to the SMC enhancer containing rs4887091: Hi-C identified a boundary loop containing ADAMTS7, MORF4L1, CHRNA3, IDH3A, ACSBG1, CIB2, SH2D7 and TBC1D2 promoters (Fig. 4d), whereas scE2G identified ADAMTS7 (the nearest gene) (Fig. 4g). Consistent with ADAMTS7 being a functional target of this regulatory element, CRISPRi Perturb–seq targeting the rs4887091-containing enhancer reduced ADAMTS7 expression in HCASMCs (Extended Data Fig. 8f). CTCF ChIP–seq in HCASMCs demonstrated that rs4887091 overlaps a CTCF binding site (Fig. 4g). Furthermore, motif-based transcription factor binding site analysis found that rs4887091, which changes the reference (T) to alternate (C) allele, is predicted to create a core CTCF binding motif (Fig. 4h). Consistent with this prediction, haplotype-resolved CTCF ChIP–seq demonstrated allelic dosage-dependent increases in CTCF occupancy on the C allele (P = 0.0003) (Fig. 4i). Validation at control loci and orthogonal TaqMan genotyping confirmed the accuracy of the haplotype-resolved CTCF occupancy measurements (Extended Data Fig. 10h–j). Together, these data support a model in which rs4887091 creates an allele-specific CTCF binding site associated with increased local chromatin loop strength, although the effect of this loop alteration on gene expression remains to be established.

Although our scE2G predictions are limited to enhancer–gene interactions within a cis-window, leveraging Hi-C data can link CAD GWAS variants to distal genes. For the loops present in all 15 samples, we catalogued genes linked to a CAD GWAS variant through direct chromatin contact between putative enhancers and promoters and identified 11 such genes: ANTXR1, ARMC12, CNNM2, FKBP5, CAPG, SH2D6, AMOTL2, NUAK2, RGS1, PLCL1 and FOXC2 (Fig. 5a). Among these, ANTXR1, CAPG, SH2D6, AMOTL2, NUAK2 and RGS1 are not the nearest genes. As an example, the CAD-associated variant rs9876658 was linked to AMOTL2 through a direct Hi-C contact. rs9876658 falls within a snATAC–seq peak in SMCs, endothelial cells and fibroblasts (but not myeloid cells) highlighting stroma-specific regulation (Fig. 5b). H3K27ac ChIP–seq showed that rs9876658 overlapped a H3K27ac peak in SMCs but not in endothelial cells (Fig. 5b). Hi-ChIP–seq further identified a direct loop between the rs9876658-containing enhancer and the AMOTL2 promoter in SMCs but not in endothelial cells (Fig. 5b). Collectively, these analyses predict that the enhancer containing rs9876658 functionally regulates expression of AMOTL2 in SMCs but not in endothelial cells.
