#979. Succumbing to certainty is a failure in science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dom Byrne is a freelance radio and podcast producer based in Brighton, UK.

Scientists should resist political pressure to provide certainty when the evidence suggests otherwise, says Andy Stirling.Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript

Science’s greatest failure is not getting things wrong, but by sometimes pretending that there is more certainty than there really is, says social scientist Andy Stirling.

This can happen, he says, when researchers face political pressure to provide a single, definitive answer, when the evidence is far more complex.

In the final episode of a six-part podcast series about failure in science, Stirling, an emeritus professor at the University of Sussex in Brighton, UK, draws on examples from climate change, the COVID-19 pandemic, environmental campaigns and energy policy.

“In those areas, science just does not convey the degree of uncertainty and of variability and of how many potentially viable options are being cut out when you just give one clear answer,” he says. “It thinks it’s helping society by just giving one picture of the truth. And in fact, it’s undermining both itself and democracy when it does that.”

Stirling, whose research includes science and technology policy and environmental politics, says that on occasions politicians have almost literally hidden behind scientists on a podium, who have relied on their authority and expertise to protect them.

Earlier this year, Stirling spoke at a one-day conference on failure in science, with a focus on careers and innovation. It was held at Imperial College London in partnership with Nature.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03837-y

Well, my failure is to take my own advice.

The thing I want to say here, I, you know, talk the talk.

I’m big on talking the talk, but walking the walk is tricky.

That’s social scientist Professor Andy Stirling at the opening session of the Failure in Science conference, held at Imperial College London in April 2026.

It’s why I’m so motivated. I’ll create a false frisson of expectation.

It’s why I’m so motivated to say what I’m going to say in this panel that it is so difficult.

Up until now, in this series, we’ve talked about individual scientists seeing failure come their way.

And we’ve talked about science institutions, universities, trying to get good at allowing failure as part and parcel of science.

But as a social scientist peering at science through that lens, Professor Stirling takes this a step further.

I’m trying to contribute with many others to a move towards making it okay to speak about how the results we get in science are never, even when we are massively successful, never mind when we’re failing.

They are never as singular, and unambiguous, and definitive as our disciplines, our superiors, and policymakers force us to pretend.

If science is supposed to exist for the betterment of humanity, is it actually doing a good job?

Does science fail sometimes or often when it heads out into society?

I’m Dr Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial College London, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don’t.

In episode six, we explore how the very project of science sometimes fails our society, and we discuss how it could adapt to better serve its citizens.

We’re asking, how can good science and good science policy benefit from admitting that sometimes we don’t really know?

What we’re discussing here, of course, is science and democracy, where we like to believe everyone has their say.

Well, my name’s Andy Stirling, and I’m a professor at the University of Sussex, and visiting or honorary at UCL and Leiden.

Given that my topic is on how science functions in society, one of my best candidates, I think, for a failure is just being so slow to realize how power works around science.

I’ve spent years, you know, chipping in in modest ways on advisory processes, advisory committees on this and that topic because of the nature of the work I do, and it took me a long time to realize just how powerful the forces are that pressurize science into giving certain kinds of answers, or not asking certain kinds of questions.

Those forces are much more powerful than I had thought at the beginning. Even though I thought of myself quite hard-nosed, I’ve really been quite surprised.

Sure, yeah. Well, look, it was a fantastic conference all around different aspects of failure, and that was in the context of a lot of people talking really eloquently about failure within science, and actually how science can benefit and people can benefit from failure.

So that was a context for me picking up that science itself has, in an important sense, failed itself and society.

And in saying that, I absolutely didn’t say it out of a spirit of being critical of science.

It’s because I am so enthusiastic. I regard science as so precious that the disappointment, as it were, of that is all the more acute when you value science in society.

And I said it because, in a nutshell, I think science fails to communicate the most important thing about itself to society, and that matters because the times in which people are most listening to science is when there’s some kind of crisis about climate, about some sort of technology that’s causing a risk, about what to do with future innovation.

So on those areas, science just does not convey the degree of uncertainty and of variability and of how many potentially viable options are being cut out when you just give one clear answer.

It thinks it’s helping society by just giving one picture of the truth.

And in fact, it’s undermining both itself and democracy when it does that.

You’ll probably want to unpack what I mean by all that, but that’s the nutshell.

So yeah, I think it is useful to see science as a social movement. That’s not the only way to see it. There’s all kinds of different views. It’s in the spirit of my, what I’m trying to say that there are different ways of viewing this one thing.

But all the more important because it gets neglected.

Science is very often as much by critics sometimes as by its protagonists, put forward in any given area as being some objective source of authority, a definitive authority.

And even if uncertainties are acknowledged, there’s a kind of disembodied, detached idea of scientific expertise.

And one can understand that. I mean, I say this in the spirit of really respecting how amazing the transcendent kind of progress can be in areas by really applying scientific method.

But we tend to forget that science is itself located in society.

So the kinds of questions that it asks, the kinds of resources that are applied, the kinds of attitudes that it takes when it’s challenged or when it’s trying to influence, is very human, subject to all kinds of interest.

I mean, how often do scientists display enormous enthusiasm about their particular field, often their particular technology?

They’re highly partisan. It comes with the ability to be highly critical. It doesn’t, it’s not separate.

There’s certain questions won’t be asked for many years unless you get different disciplines together, and then they’ll ask each other more difficult questions. But often they won’t even talk to each other.

So yeah, it’s a social movement. It’s a collection of social movements, and by that I mean, I mean it’s got all kinds of institutions and organizations and cultures in it.

But maybe a good way to illustrate this is the Royal Society, one of the first in the modern idea of science in the world.

Their motto in the 17th century was nullius in verba. Not on anyone’s word, not on authority.

And it is deliciously ironic when you see now these enormous reports on nuclear or geoengineering or gene editing being slapped down on the table with the motto nullius in verba, when in fact it is being used as a source of authority.

But the the foundation of science, it was a reaction to doctrinal assertions from the monarchy or from the church.

And scientists were saying we want to argue about it. We want to have experiments. We want to have analysis. We want to have reasoned arguments about how you can draw different conclusions.

And of course, in the beginning, that was highly exclusive. It was old white males.

But nonetheless, the principle was you should be able to argue with each other, irrespective of your authority.

And now, I’m afraid, science is often a little bit seduced by power and privilege. It gets locked into patronage networks so that, you know, it gets rewarded, and too often it sees itself as a source of authority rather than a source of questions.

When we say with climate change, what does the, what does, do what the science says.

There are a lot of activists come out with banners saying that, but also you know chief scientists often find themselves saying something similar.

And you can’t because the science says nothing without values and interests to help frame it.

There’s nothing about evidence and data in the climate area as anywhere else that actually compels you to act in a particular way.

It’s really crucial. I say this as somebody who’s worked on climate since the 80s, but it’s not the science that tells us what to do.

It’s also the science, along with values and interests and experience, that helps us shape and frame the science that really matters.

And why that matters is we basically block the politics out. And we block out that you can get different answers from the same data by asking the question differently or different questions.

And if we block that out, what we’re doing is being authoritarian, because we’re just giving one answer.

We’re hiding the values that give you that one answer, and then for those people who don’t share those values, by doing that, we’re being authoritarian. And instead of prompting compliance, we provoke a backlash, an authoritarian backlash.

So when science laments the post-truth authoritarianism that it experiences in many areas, it’s I think to a large extent seeing itself in the mirror.

And if it was more honest about its own uncertainties, its own politics, the way there’s always different answers you could get from any given model, we might get a more reasoned debate.

If you think back to the history of environmentalism and ask when was it most successful, you know everyone will have different views of this.

It’s in the spirit of my analysis that there’s different stories to be told.

But whether it’s whales, pesticides, chlorine chemicals, heavy metals. Although none of these issues have finally been won, there were some major victories took place in the history of environmentalism, rightly or wrongly, in which things were withdrawn from.

And across the board, the way that was done was against science, quite often expert scientists, academics, industry, government, universities, saying, "Look, we’ve done the science. It’s okay. We’ve done the calculations. We have models of the dispersion in the ocean."

And the environmentalists said, "We don’t believe your science. We think it’s been shaped by the kinds of power around it.

"And we’re talking about values. It’s just wrong to do this. And if you look at your model in a different way, you’ll get a different answer. You’ll get the answer we get."

And then again and again and again, environmentalists won on that kind of argument. By the time you roll around as as science and also especially environmentalism become institutionalized, you get exactly the arguments that lost being deployed in favour of climate change.

We’ve done the models. We’re global. We’ve modeled the entire global climate system. We thought up something called global mean temperature.

We are insisting it should be static, when in fact we know it’s dynamic, and we’re defining it to very high degrees of precision and saying our models will be the means by which the world addresses this problem.

So rather than doing it in terms of virtues and values and the kind of society we want to live in, which lost in the past.

We’re doing it on do what the science says, which lost in the past, arguably rightly, because you can’t do what the science says, and in the process we’re provoking exactly the backlash, as I mentioned earlier.

So that’s an example of the kinds of ways it’s been lost. That climate is of absolutely crucial importance, but it should be recognized to be a struggle, a democratic struggle, and not just based on science, because that’s the way you actually lose issues, not win them.

To behave like that is itself post-truth.

When science downplays its uncertainties, downplays the sensitivities, the way in which different assumptions in the model, which are equally reasonable, could get a different answer, the way in which values, emotions, virtues, ideologies all play a role in science, just like they do outside.

When it pretends that’s not the case, it is in fact behaving in a post-truth way, and so then it’s not surprising it gets a post-truth reaction.

So doubling down on that is exactly...it’s like throwing kerosene on the fire. It’s just not going to work to. Your self behaving in this authoritarian way and expect other authoritarianisms to go away.

We should be informing democracy and achieving these changes through democratic struggle. And science is absolutely essential to that, but only if it conducts itself in an honest way.

One thing that got me going with all this was in back in the ’90 s I was looking at risk assessments, cost-benefit analysis, life cycle assessments.

All these highly technical quantitative assessments in the energy sector.

Cutting a long story short, they were, the energy sector was the place where these things were developed to their most mature, sophisticated form. And if you looked at any given study, you got this really confident idea.

This is what the risks of nuclear are compared to renewables, compared to gas, or whatever it is.

The same with the other methods I mentioned.

And then every single time you stand back and you look at the literature as a whole, not just peer-reviewed literature, but the literature embodied in law.

So the most kind of authoritatively treated source of data on these things, and you found you could get any answer you like across that peer-reviewed literature.

It depends on the framing. The models give you an answer that depends on how you frame the question.

And that for me kind of radicalized me because I realized that none of the committees, none of the reports around the world were fully representing what the literature they were consulting told us, that you can get all kinds of different answers.

And what matters is not just the one answer, the risk, the cost, environmental costs, the ecosystem service.

What matters is how that changes depending on assumptions, that’s how science should speak to policy, but also to society, telling us how these things depend.

The reason I said that, a lot of people talk about lamenting the fact we have policy-based evidence rather than evidence-based policy, and it’s a good point.

You know, you get all kinds of practices making things up all the time, all over the place in every sector.

But my point wasn’t to lambast that. It wasn’t to say, to lament yet again "you guys are just stitching it up." It was to say "Actually, I’ve never yet seen an area where the evidence compels a single policy."

So even when you do get the best quality evidence, it is never without uncertainties. It’s never without differences of implication for action, depending on which discipline was actually most influential, how the questions were asked, what the baselines were, etc. etc.

So I have yet to see any body of analysis based on evidence that compels a single decision.

So when you hear people talking about evidence-based policy as if there were only one policy that could have been based on the evidence, they’re basically again being post-truth.

They’re (to be a bit more colourful about it, they’re telling porkies."

Because there will always be values, interests, assumptions at work, and it’s not a bad thing. It’s inevitable.

That’s how science, you know, depends. For instance, on BSE whether vets or were the epidemiologists in charge? He got a very different answer.

And in COVID, you know, again, we-I mean, it’s still too early to say, as Mao said, I think about the French Revolution, was it? But it’s too early to say.

But you can still see that what was the best way to act on the available evidence, economic as well as epidemiological, and the different ways of interpreting the epidemiological evidence.

It’s very clear now that it’s not so clear-cut what a particular country should do.

Different countries do different things. There are different ways of looking back on it, looking at the time and seeing what was good and what was bad.

So, without taking position on either side, it’s far from clear that there was a single definitive action that should have been taken.

I defy anyone to actually come back and defend that. There’ll be a matter of judgment as between really quite radically different policies.

So COVID is an example of this. I think we had to pretend there was one policy because it was so stressful.

Politicians had to pretend because otherwise they would have to hide behind their chief scientists, literally sometimes, literally behind them on the podium, hiding behind them because they needed that authority to protect them from the inevitable uncertainties that everyone believed were really there, even though they weren’t acknowledging it in the graphs.

I mean, blame management, trust, public acceptance.

These things are the most important commodities in politics. So yeah, and it’s you know apocryphally, people have all kinds of anecdotes out on these advisory committees.

I’ve served a little bit on some of them. You know, the number of times in which the politicians will intimate, "I won’t hesitate to hide behind you," almost as a joke.

But so you know, scientists respond to that in different ways. But by and large, they think, "Well, okay, we’ve got to be responsible. Let’s give these guys a single prescriptive answer, even though we know among ourselves that we could have got a different answer, but we’ve got a responsibility not to do an to do to do an elevator pitch."

You know, not to give on the one hand, on the other, as Margaret Thatcher said, "Save me from the two-handed economist. I want a one-handed economist."

She wants it because of justification, but actually, it’s a responsibility of the economist, or in this case, a scientist, to actually explain how it does depend. It always does depend.

If they don’t explain that, then they are failing, I would say science, and failing society, failing democracy.

Other things are really complicated. there’s a lot of real challenges. I don’t want to pretend it’s easier than it really is.

But actually, we shouldn’t be paralyzed by this. Look at science itself. When it developed in the 17th century, motto of the Royal Society, nullius in verba, that was basically saying that principles of accountability, of argument, of deliberation really mattered, of treating people more equally than many institutions do. That’s not the opposite of democracy. That is democracy.

Science was about, in many ways, democratizing knowledge.

You know, you needed to argue, you need to show evidence and do analyzes in rigorous ways. But it should be open to anyone to do that, and to any perspective, no matter how ridiculous it sounds, if it can substantiate itself.

So science and democracy are not on opposite sides.

So I think, rather than counterpointing them, like science is against democracy, we can’t trust democracy, going to undermine science, actually, see it the other way round: that science is an embodiment of democracy.

It’s when it is at its best. It’s when it’s being democratic about the ability to challenge power inside science, and that’s how we solve the problems of science.

It’s also how we solve the problems at the moment of democracy, which science is, sadly, because it’s forced to be more authoritarian in pretending a singular truth.

It’s forced into that not by democracy, but by power that is also eroding democracy.

Science, when it comes to advise policymakers, yes, please do your best, but don’t think of yourself just giving a single expedient answer so that a politician goes away happy and can act without worrying about blame.

Inform society at large about the assumptions that went into that.

Show how it depends, and if you do that, you’re informing democracy as much as the powerful actors who are, you know, maybe conferring the patronage on the scientists.

Science fails when it’s not being plural enough.

It needs to be plural about who’s involved, about the questions that are asked, about the disciplines that get around the table, about how it conveys its interpretations of its understandings out to society, and it needs to just not be scared of representing that plurality because with that comes the conditions.

It’s not just anything goes. It’s not plural for plurality’s sake.

It’s then saying under what conditions you get answer X or answer Y, and that’s more scientific.

It’s more rigorous to behave in that way.

When science does that, it’s being more scientific when it’s plural. So I think science fails most when it reduces all those kinds of plurality.

#978. Preparing for 45C: How Germany tests its crisis response

A record heat wave. Five years of drought. A nation under pressure. Germany is running its biggest joint crisis exercise to date to test how authorities would cope with an escalating climate emergency.

Imagine a situation in which prolonged drought has devastated Germany and much of Europe, taking a toll on people's lives, the environment and economy — with a heat wave with temperatures of up to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit) compounding the situation.

About 180 organizations across Germany, including more than 60 ministries at the state level and nearly 20 federal authorities, are taking part in a major crisis exercise known as LÜKEX 26, which is built around this very scenario.

It is Germany's cross-government crisis management exercise organized by the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK). And it's been up and running for more than two decades.

The first LÜKEX in 2004 dealt with the scenario of an extreme winter with a major power outage. Lessons from that exercise proved valuable in 2005 when the Münsterland region of North Rhine-Westphalia — Germany's most populous state — experienced the worst power outage in the country's postwar history. When heavy snowfall caused power lines to collapse, leaving 250,000 people without electricity for days, there was a better understanding of who to contact and where the bottlenecks were.

Since it first started, LÜKEX has trained for scenarios involving terror attacks, an influenza pandemic, biological health threats, storm floods in northern Germany and gas shortages in southern Germany. The most recent exercise in 2023 simulated a cyberattack targeting government operations.

With the help of other ministries, the German Weather Service and the Federal Institute of Hydrology, the BBK developed a drought risk analysis to serve as the scenario.

Participants, which include aid organizations Malteser and the German Red Cross, didn't know the specifics of the challenges they would be facing until the exercise kicked off on Wednesday.

At that point, they were told it was July 20, 2027. In that simulated future, they find themselves in a Germany that has been struggling with extreme heat for weeks; water levels in rivers are falling, food supplies are becoming scarce and emergency services are under growing pressure.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patrick Pöhler, spokesperson for Malteser, said additional details include supermarkets having run out of water, collapsed supply chains and skyrocketing prices to enter a swimming pool. He said the scenario also goes into how the situation is impacting sections of society.

"Emergency services and elderly care are areas that require particular attention," Pöhler said. "The increasingly extreme summers of recent years have shown how severely heat can affect staffing levels and operational capacity."

In its scenario, the northern port city of Hamburg is tasked with managing the disruption of key transport routes that are impacting access to food and drinking water, as well as handling disinformation attacks that are fueling public fear.

"We have not conducted an exercise of this magnitude since the end of the Cold War. Yet such preparations are essential to strengthen our resilience and crisis-response capabilities," said Hamburg's minister for the interior, Andy Grote.

LÜKEX is designed to test and strengthen the country's ability to manage major crises at a strategic level. No matter the specific scenario, they all help test internal structures, workflows and decision-making processes.

"The lessons learned are continuously incorporated into improving preparedness, planning and cooperation in civil protection," said BBK spokesperson Katharina Böcker.

This year's topic was decided a long time ago, well before recent summers in which Germany experienced extreme heat, she added. Thousands of people died from heat-related causes during the hot months of this year.

"Crises such as extreme heat waves and prolonged droughts can affect large parts of the population and challenge the operational capabilities of our critical structures over an extended period," said Christian Reuter, secretary general of the German Red Cross, another organization taking part.

Observers take note of how organizations react in the crisis scenario to find out what went well and where things didn't run smoothly.

"We are explicitly encouraged to make mistakes," said Malteser's Pöhler, because that is how weaknesses can be identified and addressed.

A first internal debrief is scheduled for Friday, he added.

A preliminary report with the main findings and respective recommendations is due to be published in the first quarter of next year. A full evaluation report will then be released later in the third quarter of 2027.

#977. 'You can't escape from it': Rasmus Hojlund opens up on the suffocating pressure of playing for Man United - and reveals Bruno Fernandes and Diogo Dalot are 'looking forward to change' under Mauricio Pochettino

Published: 05:31 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 06:12 EST, 25 November 2026

Rasmus Hojlund has laid bare the suffocating pressure of playing for Manchester United and given his insight into what Mauricio Pochettino’s squad will be suffering while marooned in the Premier League relegation zone.

The Dane was back in town this week after spending two seasons at United, mocking Manchester City fans when scoring the opener of Napoli’s 2-2 draw at the Etihad Stadium on Tuesday night.

Hojlund secured a £38million permanent move away from Old Trafford in the summer but remains in touch with plenty of old team-mates and believes the lack of equilibrium at the club has contributed to a steady decline.

‘There are so many people following the club around the world and you can’t really escape from it,’ Hojlund said.

‘It is almost too high when it is good and almost too low when it is bad. It is all about trying to be in that middle. I had both the highs and the lows there.

‘The pressure is part of the club, it comes with playing for United. There has been a lot of change but hopefully they will get it right with Mauricio.’

Rasmus Hojlund mocked Man City fans after scoring for Napoli at the Etihad on Tuesday night

A United supporter, Hojlund laughed off the idea that the club is in a relegation scrap despite their worst start to a season since 1972. And the 23-year-old revealed that the players were ready for ‘change’ following the sacking of Michael Carrick.

‘I spoke with Bruno [Fernandes] and Diogo [Dalot] during the international break and they were all obviously devastated that Michael was going but also looking forward to some change,’ Hojlund added.

‘I am still speaking with Patrick [Dorgu] and I just wish the guys all the best. I am sure they will turn it around this season. They have got a lot of quality. They have got a great squad, good leaders, good professionals.

‘It is a temporary picture, I think they will get back to the top. The Premier League is like this. I read the other day that Bournemouth was in the relegation zone after a couple of games, now they have won the last five games and are in the top half of the table.’

#975. Odegaard winner spares officials from bizarre VAR row

An ultimately routine Arsenal win but, even by the standards of VAR, an utterly bizarre refereeing controversy. Mikel Arteta’s instant simmering fury at being denied a first-half penalty may also have turned into something rather more explosive had Martin Odegaard not later sent the champions six points clear with a ninth win in 10 Premier League games.

The big talking point arose with inadvertent theatre from referee Farai Hallam when Kai Havertz, who was clearly in an offside position, was equally clearly pulled down by Hull City defender Nobel Mendy inside the penalty area. Which came first? The intervention of VAR suggested the latter. But Hallam duly went to check the pitch-side monitor before then announcing the former.

“After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No 32 on Red No 29,” the referee declared. Cue cheers from the home Arsenal crowd. “However…,” he went on. “Red No 29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City.”

#ARSHUL – 42' VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty to Arsenal for a challenge by Mendy on Havertz - but determined that Havertz was in an offside position in the build-up. REF: "After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No.32 on Red No.29. However, Red No.29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City".

It all sounded so decisive that most inside the Emirates instinctively thought the outcome reasonable. But then came a closer look at the rules. And Law 11.2 certainly did seem to support Arteta’s protestations: “In situations where a player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”

Arteta clearly saw no value after the match in aiming much criticism at Hallam following a fourth 1-0 win in 10 league games, but did still emphasise his surprise at the decision. “What do you think?” he asked one reporter. “I thought offside, but the law says that doesn’t matter,” replied the journalist. “So not offside then,” said Arteta, who stressed that he needs to understand “what is overruling what in the decision-making” after a Premier League statement simply said that Havertz was deemed offside “in the build-up”.

At the very best, it all leaves further confusion and again opens refereeing body Pro Ref to the charge of inconsistency. Fabian Schär, for example, was awarded a penalty for Newcastle against Bournemouth in 2024, despite being in an offside position when his shirt was grabbed by Adam Smith.

Conversely, Dango Ouattara had a penalty overturned for Brentford against Leeds last season after going down under pressure from Gabriel Gudmundsson before being deemed offside. The crucial point seems to be whether the player has actually challenged for the ball at the time of the infringement and, in this case, the answer was surely “no”.

Premier League title triumphs, however, are often forged on forgettable wins in frustrating circumstances and this was ultimately a classic of the genre. With Noni Madueke continuing to step up superbly in the absence of Bukayo Saka, Arsenal’s combination of attacking persistence and defensive resilience was ultimately rewarded by Odegaard’s scrappy 72nd-minute shot. For young players, it was also every bit as educational as the VAR controversy might be for emerging officials.

Madueke’s low shot forced a save by Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis, but Odegaard was somehow first to the rebound, despite being the wrong side of the penalty spot and five yards behind Hull defender John Egan when the ball was struck.

“The way he scores, not the most beautiful, but the most effective,” said Arteta, who said that his team had sometimes tried too hard for a “perfect goal” and should instead be happy with something “more pragmatic”.

It was a well-judged assessment as Arsenal head into the international break with creative deficiencies, but still almost flawless in the cold hard currency of results. Three wins in three days, including at Anfield and in Prague, also underlines a certain champions mentality.

“I need to praise the players,” said Arteta. “It’s been very very demanding; very short time to recover with all the travel. The mentality is incredible. It’s still going to be super difficult. We can improve in a number of areas.”

When it was then put to him that Arsenal have been offside 35 times this season – with Havertz responsible for 15 of those – Arteta acknowledged that “timing” was one element. But, with Havertz targeted by some frustrated fans, he stressed that responsibility was always shared for those split-second moments by the passer and receiver.

He also singled out Madueke, again easily Arsenal’s most creative player, following his surprise omission from Thomas Tuchel’s England squad. “He went away, started to train, he came back and it was a different Noni,” said Arteta, of his reaction to also being out of the Arsenal team earlier in the season. “You could sense that he meant business and he wasn’t going to accept the situation and, since then, I think he’s been incredible.”

An improved showing by Jaissle’s Newcastle, but they will be dissapointed that they failed to see it through after Jacob Murphy scored in the 80th minute.

Arsenal far from their best, but it is another one-goal win in the Premier League. They are now six points clear at the top of the Premier League, and it is 27 points from the first 30 available.

Another save at Craven Cottage, this time from Hornicek to keep out a sweet strike from Sessegnon at the edge of the box. Moments earlier, Dedic brought down Muniz at the edge of the box.

One last change by Arteta: Zubmimendi on for Guimaraes. Madueke could have made the points safe after slick interplay involving Eze and Merino around the edge of the box. Tried to be clever with the finish, the goalkeeper’s save was deflected back towards the goal and it was hacked off the line.

Leno gets down quickly to deny Lewis Hall as Newcastle pour forward in search of the winner.

As good as Murphy’s goal was, Rodrigo Muniz’s finish with the outside of his foot may well be better. Newcastle’s lead was short-lived.

And they have immediately conceded an equaliser, Rodrigo Munoz with a smart close range finish but Newcastle were be mortified with the defending.

Not for the first time Will Osula’s weak hold up play gives the ball back to Fulham but Newcastle had plenty of men back and failed to clear.

Jacob Murphy has scored the goal that some of Newcastle’s earlier good play deserved. Cut inside on to his weaker left foot, and curled a shot beyond Leno from 20 yards.

Newcastle finally have their goal and what a strike it is from Jacob Murphy. A loose pass from Cesar Palacios in midfield gifted possession to the Newcastle winger and he ran forward, cut inside on to his left foot and curled a shot beyond the reach of Leno from 25 yards.

Arsenal’s captain dinks over Tzolakis after Hull’s goalkeeper saved Madueke’s shot. Odeegard was on the move while the defenders were on their heels. Relief at the Emirates, this has been hard work for the champions. Can Hull muster a response?

This is about as dominant as Newcastle have been in a game all season but they have not been able to find a goal from some where. They have just gone close again as Will Osula just fails to reach Amar Dedic’s cross.

Arteta has made another double sub: Hincapie and Eze replace Tzolis and Calafiori, so all change down the left flank. For Hull, Lucas Herrington has replaced the injured Semi Ajayi at the back.

Felt like the cheers for Viktor Gyokeres to replace Kai Havertz were as much a reflection on frustrations with the German as enthusiasm for the Swede. Havertz has struggled today and is far less convincing in this sort of match – when the onus is more on the Arsenal to create – than he was in scoring the winner at Anfield last Sunday.

Specific explanation for Declan Rice’s substitution is unclear – he didn’t look injured – and so perhaps just reflection of risks associated with a third 90 minutes in six days alongside an acknowledgement of quality alternatives on the bench.

Some changes at the Emirates: Cho and Lewie Coyle are replaced by Joe Gelhardt and Brooke Norton-Cuffy.

Arteta with a double sub: Gyokeres and Merino on for Havertz and Rice, which comes as something of a surprise.

Hull’s goalkeeper Tzolakis has just saved with his feet to deny Madueke. A few minutes earlier, Konsa blocked a Cho shot after a threatening Hull break. Still no opening goal.

It has been all Newcastle at the start of the second half and Harvey Barnes has now failed to take a hat-trick of chances. This was the best of the lot, running on to the ball, middle of the area from a perfectly weighted Yoane Wissa pass, he blasted a shot the wrong side of the post.

The second halves at the Emirates and Craven Cottage have kicked off. No changes from Arsenal, Hull, Fulham or Newcastle.

While Kai Havertz was in an offside position when his shirt was pulled, he may not have been active.

The law states: “A player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”

However, the Premier League match centre does not see it that way.

#ARSHUL – 42' VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty to Arsenal for a challenge by Mendy on Havertz - but determined that Havertz was in an offside position in the build-up. REF: "After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No.32 on Red No.29. However, Red No.29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City".

Frustrating first half for Arsenal, but it was never going to be easy to go again in the Premier League following a Champions League away game and last Sunday’s big win against Liverpool. Hull have also played with confidence and resolve.

Hopefully there will be more action in the second 45 minutes at Craven Cottage and the Emirates.

An odd moment at the Emirates. Referee Farai Hallam was sent to monitor to look at a shirt pull on Kai Havertz in the Hull box. Through his headset, he tells the crowd that a “holding offence” has been committed – cue cheers from the Arsenal fans – before adding “however, the Arsenal player was in an offside position”. So no penalty. It would have been very soft in any case, Havertz was not close to reaching the rebound from a long shot.

Mikel Arteta predictably furious to not get a penalty, even though Havertz was clearly offside before being pulled.

I’ve spotted something else since I was covering Arsenal in 2018. I was gazing up at the boards that circle the top tier where the club mark every trophy that the team has won. There was previously this big gap, of course, from 2005 until 2014 before the cabinet gradually began refilling. But someone has since had a good idea. They have added all the women’s trophies as well, transforming the tally by just the odd 17 during those tricky years of transition and billionaire rivals owners in the men’s game.

Declan Rice has also just had a shot flash wide, but still no clear chances for either team.

Dan Burn thought he had scored from close-range, but Wissa has been penalised for blocking Castagne so the goal was ruled out.

#FULNEW – 33' The referee's call of no goal to Newcastle United was checked and confirmed by VAR – with it deemed that Wissa fouled Castagne in the build-up. AR2: "Defensive foul at the back post. Wissa holding at the back post". REF: "Castagne held back by Wissa. It's a deliberate foul". VAR: "He's clearly holding him - confirming the on-field decision of defensive free-kick. Wissa is clearly making an attempt to hold the Fulham defender. Clear holding offence".

Some controversy here as Newcastle appear to have had a perfectly good goal ruled out for an innocuous looking foul from Yoane Wissa on Timothy Costagne inside the box. Dan Burn was the scorer. Newcastle’s bench are furious. Most of us are just bemused.

Arsenal have largely been on top after Hull’s lively start but clear chances are scarce and Hull’s fans certainly sound increasingly confident. “You’re only here for the Tigers”, they say. To which a rendition of “champions” rings out. On that note, they had a replica of the Premier League trophy outside the Emirates before the match, with fans queuing up to get their photo with it.

The bright start from the visitors has not been maintained and Fulham have been on top for the last few minutes. Lukasz Hornicek just made a full-stretch save to deny Oscar Bobb and there is a sense inside the stadium that the first goal is coming.

Newcastle, as we have seen all too often recently, really struggle to pass through the lines and when the ball makes it out wide it invariably seems to go backwards again.

Although Harvey Barnes has just forced a good save from Leno from a Jacob Murphy cross. It was easily Newcastle’s best move of the match as Wissa and Osula linked up for the first time through the middle.

David Raya to Arsenal’s rescue, plucking Stroud’s shot away from the bottom corner after a Calafiori giveaway. This has been a positive opening 20 minutes from Hull.

Arsenal with a penalty shout, turned down.

Mikel Arteta has said Arsenal are “looking after” Declan Rice more now than in any previous campaign and has rejected suggestions that the England midfielder is being overplayed.

Rice played through nerve pain in his hamstring in the second half of last season, when he made an extraordinary 69 appearances for club and country.

The 27-year-old has played at least 60 matches in each of the past four campaigns, prompting concerns among Arsenal supporters that he is at risk of burnout or injury.

Asked if he was concerned about Rice’s fitness, Arteta said: “Concerns? Which is the only player, the only player in this squad, that for two games in the Carabao Cup has been left out of the squad? At home with two days off? It’s not true [that Rice is being overplayed].

#974. Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck

Elon Musk's electric pickup for the future will start to be consigned to the past next year. The Cybertruck's bulk and crude shape meant it could only pass regulatory standards in more permissive markets.

Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the company would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.

The South African entrepreneur said Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.

"Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said on his X social media site.

The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections, where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

Musk later responded to a complimentary user online who hailed the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made," and calling it an "end of an era" by saying: "True."

For years he had poured much of his enthusiastic marketing zeal into promoting the Cybertruck, saying during the 2023 launch "finally, the future will look like the future."

However the oversized body, straight lines and stainless steel and the post-apocalpytic vibe these created also met with widespread criticism and even mockery.

The electric powertrain was probably a barrier to sales in the US, by far the biggest pickup truck market, where Musk had hoped to take on some of the country's top-selling gas-guzzling vehicles like the Ford F150 or the Chevrolet Silverado and the Dodge Ram.

Meanwhile, the car's striking shape, weight and size made it impossible for Tesla to try to crack Europe, where electric vehicles are gaining a much larger market share.

Unlike in the US, EU safety regulations place considerable emphasis not just on people in cars in accidents, but also on the dangers posed to pedestrians who might be hit by a vehicle. That meant it was not possible for Tesla to register and sell the Cybertruck for road use in Europe.

Beyond this, the vehicle's size would likely have rendered it impractical and unpopular on many European roads, where space tends to be at more of a premium.

Depending how quick the wind-down proves to be, the Cybertruck's production run could prove shorter than its five-year R&D phase.

Given its longstanding issues meeting Musk's very public sales and production predictions, Tesla does not publish sales figures broken down by model.

But according to the automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024.

At launch in 2023, Musk had predicted unit sales nearer a quarter of a million.

For orientation, Ford sold more than 800,000 F-Series pickups in the US last year, a slight boost on 2024's numbers. These vehicles start at less than half the list price of a Cybertruck in the US.

The IPO for SpaceX this year revealed that Musk's second-largest company was comfortably the biggest buyer of Cybertrucks in 2025. It bought vehicles worth $131 million and did not even enjoy a bulk-buy or friends-rate discount, paying list prices for the fleet.

The Cybercab is a vehicular element in Musk's bid to transform Tesla towards a company focused more on AI and robotics than automobilies.

Rather than just featuring the self-drive or driving assistance programs that Musk has been championing for years, the Cybercab has no steering wheels, pedals or mirrors at all and is designed never to have a human in control.

Musk say the model will be the company's main autonomous model and will supply a global network of Robotaxis.

Starting in the past few months, around 300 such vehicles have been registered and have started operating, on approved roads in the Austin area near Tesla's Gigafactory Texas. They're being added to the existing fleet of autonomous Model Y Teslas being used for the purpose, serving in an area known as a geofence of around 680 square kilometers (264 square miles).

#972. Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability

France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he said.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire."

"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales."

Their common message, he said, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts."

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

"In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.

This article was originally written in German.

Oliver Glasner has played down the significance of his warning to Nottingham Forest’s squad after their defeat at Brentford has had the desired impact.

The Austrian said last weekend there would be “no compromises” and insisted his players have to fully buy into his philosophy.

Speaking this week, he said: “I didn’t attack anyone directly. We share that we want to be successful and win games. It was not a problem.

“It was much louder outside than I felt it was inside. This is just how I see a relationship has to be. Let’s talk about things if we don’t like things.

“If you never say anything in your relationship with your wife or children, then they will never know. Then I can’t blame somebody because if they don’t know, how can you expect things to change?

“We are now in a society where criticism or the way I talk is negative, but the intention was positive and to change to get better results so that we can all have a better life.”

Gianluigi Donnarumma, who has made three errors leading to goals this season, “recognises that he has made some mistakes,” Enzo Maresca said this week, “but at the same time recognises that he has made some great saves”.

The City manager added: “It is quite easy with him because he recognises any mistake immediately. I’ve spoken to him about it, but I didn’t feel the need to be so deep with him because he already knows and recognises that he has made some mistakes.”

Asked about City players adapting to his philosophy, Maresca said: “I can see my playing style just by working every day with them, but we can still improve many things.

“We know exactly what we are doing well and what we need to improve. It is just a matter of time.”

Elsewhere this afternoon, Martin Odegaard has broken the deadlock at the Emirates to give Arsenal a 1-0 lead over Hull City.

Victory would take Mikel Arteta’s side six points clear of City at the top of the table before this evening’s contest at the City Ground.

Glasner has made two changes to his Forest team following defeat at Brentford last weekend, with Yates and Munoz replacing Ndoye and Aina.

Is this the day the xG gods reward Nottingham Forest? Oliver Glasner’s team sit 19th having won one game all season, but there is no doubt that their performances have been significantly better than results and they might need their luck to turn against Man City team full of firepower.

Despite all of the positive indicators in Forest’s underlying data, Glasner caused some alarm with his comments after last weekend’s defeat at Brentford.

The Austrian said: “We have to accept it’s not good enough. If we lose four of the last five games, it’s not good enough. And that’s why for me, it’s now time that we change things, that I change things, and that’s what I will do.

“I feel now maybe I made too many compromises in some stuff, and it’s always compromises. It’s a clear way. I will tell [the players] what we want to do, what we have to do, and if the players buy in, I think we can have a turnaround, and if not, the sixth manager [since the start of last season] will come in.”

Glasner has happy memories of playing City, beating them in the 2025 FA Cup final with Crystal Palace, but his Forest reign is in urgent need of a signature victory and performance.

#969. Germany hopes to host world ice hockey championship — without Russia

International protests continue after a court ruled that Russia must be allowed to return to international ice hockey. Germany is seeking a solution that will allow the country to host next year's world championship.

A government spokesman has said that, despite talks with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB), the International Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) and others, the impasse caused by last week's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling remains.

Since the October 30 decision, several leading ice hockey nations — including Finland, Sweden and Czechia — have said they would refrain from playing against Russia in any tournament in which it is allowed to take part. Several key sponsors have also threatened to pull out, should the Russians be allowed to play.

The first tournament to be affected would be the Men's World Juniors, which opens in Canada in late December, followed by the IIHF's premier event, the Men's World Ice Championship, to be hosted by Germany in May.

Stefan Kornelius, the spokesman for Germany's government, told reporters in Berlin on Friday that talks held with various stakeholders had made clear that Russia's participation would render the hosting of the championship "practically impossible — both from a sporting and an economic perspective."

Kornelius said talks would continue and the government still hoped for a diplomatic solution that would allow Germany to host the championship — as planned — in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf in May.

"Our goal must be to hold the tournaments as scheduled," he said. "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Following the CAS ruling that the IIHF must allow Russia to return to international play, DEB chairman Frank Lutz had conceded that Germany may be forced to consider withdrawing as championship host.

Asked at Friday's press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman declined to answer categorically, but did indicate that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

Earlier this week, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney categorically ruled out Russian players taking part in the World Juniors in Alberta.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," he said.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors," he said, "the Russians will not be there."

Russian President Vladimir Putin has also weighed in on the issue, accusing countries opposing Russia's return to international sport of violating the rights of his country's athletes.

The IIHF Council had originally called two days of meetings, on Monday and Tuesday, to try to reach a consensus on how to respond to the CAS decision — before extending discussions for a third day, on Thursday. By Friday, its members had evidently still not reached a consensus.

This comes as the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship, which is not affected by the CAS decision, opened in Denmark — and with the clock ticking toward the start of the World Juniors in Alberta on December 26.

#967. A guide to the Nature Index

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The Nature Index is a database of author affiliations and institutional relationships. The index tracks contributions to research articles published in high-quality natural-science and health-science journals, chosen based on reputation by an independent group of researchers.

The Nature Index provides absolute and fractional counts of article publication at the institutional and national level and, as such, is an indicator of global high-quality research output and collaboration. Data in the Nature Index are updated regularly, with the most recent 12 months made available under a Creative Commons licence at natureindex.com. The database is compiled by Nature Portfolio.

The Nature Index uses Count and Share to track research output. A country/territory or an institution is given a Count of 1 for each article that has at least one author from that country/territory or institution. This is the case regardless of the number of authors an article has, and it means that the same article can contribute to the Count of multiple countries/territories or institutions.

To glean a country’s, territory’s, region’s or an institution’s contribution to an article, and to ensure that they are not counted more than once, the Nature Index uses Share, a fractional count that takes into account the share of authorship on each article. The total Share available per article is 1, which is shared among all authors under the assumption that each contributed equally. For instance, an article with 10 authors means that each author receives a Share of 0.1. For authors who are affiliated with more than one institution, the author’s Share is split equally between each institution. The total Share for an institution is calculated by summing the Share for individual affiliated authors. The process is similar for countries/territories, although complicated by the fact that some institutions have overseas labs that will be counted towards host country/territory totals.

Adjusted Share accounts for the annual variation in the total number of articles in the Nature Index journals. It is arrived at by calculating the percentage difference in the total number of articles in the Index in a given year relative to the number of articles in a base year and adjusting Share values to the base year levels.

The bilateral collaboration score (CS) between two institutions A+B is the sum of each of their Shares on the papers to which both have contributed. A bilateral collaboration can be between any two institutions or countries/territories co-authoring at least one article in the journals tracked by the Nature Index.

natureindex.com users can search for specific institutions or countries and generate their own reports, ordered by Count or Share.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03474-5

#966. Raheem Sterling's chaotic descent is a product of the cocooned world where football's little princes can't handle rejection, writes IAN HERBERT - now he must listen to those around him if he wants to salvage his career

Published: 08:21 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 11:11 EST, 25 November 2026

Raheem Sterling wore black to his sentencing hearing today, just as he had when he arrived at Basingstoke Magistrates Court two months ago and admitted to 90 minutes of terrifying rush hour driving, with canisters of nitrous oxide on the passenger seat beside him.

He was visibly more subdued this time, wearing the look of a man who’d spent two months contemplating the prospect of a jail stretch, whilst the contemporaries he once stood with in the England squad, Harry Kane, Jordan Henderson and Jordan Pickford, were continuing to hit the heights.

Imprisonment was only ever a narrow possibility under the sentencing guidelines for dangerous driving, given the miracle that Sterling did not cause serious injury or worse as he zig-zagged between lanes on the M3 and M4 that morning last May. Critically, he was not found to be under the influence of nitrous oxide. A motorist who drove in equally erratic fashion and initially ignored police on Cheshire’s M56, in a BMW which had only three tyres, was handed a suspended sentence earlier this year.

But while the mitigation preceding the magistrate’s decision that Sterling would walk free - his 12-month prison sentence is suspended for 18 months - garlanded him for his charity work and promotion of racial equality, don’t let it be said that his conduct that day was anything less than a disgrace. The tetchy hyper sensitivity Sterling displayed with the police officers who arrested him revealed a shocking lack of contrition and shame.

Sterling has had his challenges, of course. The early death of his father and a nomadic London childhood spent helping his mum on cleaning jobs. But then he disappeared into the cocooned existence of the football academy world, full of the little princes who have people fawning over them, telling them how good they are and throwing obscene amounts of money at them.

Raheem Sterling's conduct the day of his car crash was nothing short of a disgrace

Sterling's meteoric rise has meant he does not have the tools to deal with rejection

Kane has flourished in a way that Sterling hasn’t because he was forced to learn the hard way, deal with rejection and develop a sense of perspective. The princes are at the mercy of the hangers on and leeches, around them for a cut of their next big pay cheque. It was Sterling’s misfortune to select Aidy Ward as his agent – the man who conducted ugly, public contract negotiations with Liverpool which included declaring that Sterling wouldn’t be staying at Anfield even if he were offered nearly £1m a week. The reputational damage that caused Sterling should have seen him sack Ward on the spot.

The problem for those whose adolescence takes place in football’s gilded cage is that they combust and can’t hack it when the going gets remotely tough. For Sterling, read Dele Alli, Kalvin Phillips and Aaron Ramsdale.

But what makes Sterling’s personal disintegration so needless is that he really has had positive influences around him in the background. Friends who were there when he wanted to develop a voice to speak against racial discrimination in football. There when he wanted to establish a Foundation to help the kind of London teenagers that he used to be.

He lost those influences during the chaotic descent into the insanity of that spring morning when he went berserk in his car. Some of them have described to me how he flatly refused to respond to calls and went into ‘oblivion mode’ in the hours after his arrest. It seemed like he was seeking escape from any vestige of the game which is all he has known.

England captain and Sterling's former team-mate Harry Kane has thrived due to the early setbacks in his career

The tragedy is Sterling has a strong support network who want the best for him

The bleak reality for Sterling is that his career in football is surely over now. Yes, he could pick up the thread in some place below the Premier League, though his unhappy experience at Feyenoord – where there was a prurient fascination with his struggles – suggests that he will face the same relentless scrutiny wherever he goes. In the modern world, more gratuitous pleasure than ever is taken in the fall of those who were once great. It will be a circus if he pitches up somewhere new.

But the evidence of that work with boys in London suggests that he has far more of a hinterland to turn to than Alli and his ilk, if only he can re-establish those positive influences and seek help.

A moment in time, precisely two years ago, proves what his future might look like. At a meeting room in King's Cross, Sterling sat with a group of seven young men, all of whom were deemed at risk of drifting into knife crime and who had been sent along to his foundation by Brent's youth offending service.

After an initial 15 or 20 minutes when the boys seemed blinded by the superstar in their midst, they became more comfortable, seeming to feel he understood the likes of them. There were smiles as he described the various school social groups he knew. 'The cool group, the middle of the road group and the geeks,' as he called them. The 'geeks' always seemed to be a bigger part of his world when exams approached, he said with a grin. The room was wreathed with laughter, then.

The group session evolved into several one-to-one conversations between him and the boys who'd been more reticent. It was then that he pointed out the value of allowing outside mentors to help you, if your home life is challenging. 'Having someone else involved changed the course of my life,' Sterling told them.

Now is the moment when Sterling needs others to help change the course of his own life and if he accepts that, he could play a part in public life again. First comes the challenge of rousing himself from any lingering self-pity, emerging from the celebrity bubble and appreciating that he is supremely lucky to remain a free man after those abominable, mindless few hours in his souped-up car.

#965. Why Manchester United will surpass Liverpool’s title drought

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

The Red Devils are nearly halfway to matching their rivals’ 30-year title drought and there are no signs of it ending any time soon

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

“My greatest challenge was knocking Liverpool right off their f****** perch.”

Sir Alex Ferguson’s famous quote has become so embedded in football folklore that its provenance is often misremembered.

The then-Manchester United manager did not deliver the emphatic line in the early years of his tenure, as is sometimes claimed, but during a poor run of form in September 2002. The Red Devils had won seven of the previous 10 Premier League crowns, while Liverpool were not even halfway through their 30-year title drought.

Ferguson uttered that comment during Liverpool’s 13th successive campaign without winning the top flight. Fast forward almost a quarter of a century, and United are 13 years into a decline that set in as soon as the Scot retired.

The Red Devils’ title drought is already nearly half as long as the one Liverpool experienced between 1990 and 2020. They are in the Premier League relegation zone ahead of today’s trip to Anfield, so we can safely say their wait will stretch to at least the 2027/28 season, which will be 15 years since they last won the top flight.

Clearly, the 30-year mark is still a long way off and plenty can happen in that time. But it is also undeniable that United are as far from title challengers as they have been since 2013 and there are no signs of that changing.

That starts from the top. In September, executive co-chairman Avram Glazer told Deutsche Bank’s Sports Investment Conference in London that clubs of United’s stature are not dependent on success on the pitch for commercial power. The quotes, first reported by The Athletic, emerged this month when the Red Devils were about to sack manager Michael Carrick following their slide down the table.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Glazer’s comments were strikingly similar to those of former executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward in May 2018, when he told shareholders: “Playing performance doesn’t really have a meaningful impact on what we can do on the commercial side of the business.”

The fact that those two quotes occurred eight-and-a-half years apart suggests that as long as the Glazer family remain United’s majority owners, the club will prioritise commercial gain over on-pitch success.

The Americans also appear to be in no rush to sell their majority stake in the club, despite being universally unpopular with the fanbase. A report from TEAMtalk last week claimed they are unlikely to step away until United’s proposed 100,000-capacity stadium is built - which may not be until 2035 - in order to extract maximum value from their investment.

Other outlets claim the Glazers could be interested in selling their stake to co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe before then, but that certainly would not guarantee success, with the British businessman’s record in football across United, French club Nice and Swiss outfit Lausanne-Sport patchy at best.

When Ratcliffe bought a minority stake in the club in February 2024, taking control of sporting operations, it was supposed to end a decade of managerial mis-steps and overpaying for underperforming players.

However, the situation has deteriorated further, with chief executive officer Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox facing heavy criticism from fans. The Red Devils finished 15th in 2024/25 and have won just one league game this term, while the one positive half-season of the Ratcliffe era came when Carrick took over as interim boss from Ruben Amorim - another failed appointment - in January and overperformed expectations by qualifying for the Champions League.

Ultimately, United will not become a force again without an ownership change. As the Manchester United Supporters Trust (MUST) said in its statement following Carrick’s sacking: “Another change of head coach cannot repair what the ownership continues to undermine.”

This is where Liverpool’s title drought is instructive. Part of the reason for the Reds’ decline in the 1990s and 2000s was because they were overtaken financially by their rivals - initially Ferguson’s United, then Chelsea following Roman Abramovich’s takeover - under their long-time owners, the Moores family.

After the chaotic ownership of Tom Hicks and George Gillett, Fenway Sports Group (FSG) bought Liverpool in 2010. FSG did not get it right immediately, but after appointing Jurgen Klopp as manager in 2015 and putting the right people in key positions, such as sporting director Michael Edwards, the Reds were able to challenge regularly for the biggest honours again.

The team that won the title in 2020 featured some big-money recruits, most notably Virgil van Dijk and Alisson, but also several cheaper signings that resulted from a recruitment overhaul, such as Mo Salah, Roberto Firmino and Andy Robertson.

But the key point is that it took Liverpool 10 years of FSG ownership to end their title drought, and only once every department at the club, from the owners to the recruitment team to Klopp, were aligned in pursuit of on-pitch success.

It is why new United manager Mauricio Pochettino can only do so much. Like Carrick last season, Erik ten Hag in 2022/23 or Ole Gunnar Solskjaer in 2020/21, there may well be good spells during his tenure, but to paraphrase MUST, the head coach at Old Trafford will inevitably be undermined by the owners sooner or later.

Even when the Glazers eventually sell, we cannot expect the club to immediately become the force they once were, as the Liverpool example shows. It takes time to return to the top when you have been also-rans for so long.

That is why it is easy to see how United’s title drought could stretch beyond 30 years, as hypothetical as that sounds right now. If the Glazers stay in charge for the foreseeable future, the new owners would need time to undo the damage and put everything in place for success. Only then could United start to consistently challenge for the title and there is no guarantee they would win it straight away.

This scenario would have seemed unthinkable when Ferguson made his famous quip in 2002, but when you fall off your perch it is difficult to get back up - as Liverpool know all too well.

James Roberts is a freelance sports journalist working for FourFourTwo and other titles. He started his career at the Oxford Mail, where he covered Oxford United home and away, before becoming a sports sub-editor for various national newspapers.
