#953. 37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?

Three artists share their thoughts on the reunification of East and West Germany. How do they perceive a shared "we" and what gives them cause for optimism?

When the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.

Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

We asked three artists from Germany with different perspectives on the history of the country's division to share their views.

Author Lea Streisand was born in 1979 and experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall firsthand while growing up in East Berlin.

In her books and essays, she has returned to her East German upbringing many times, using literature to process it.

The novel "Hufeland, at the corner of Bötzow" (2019, Ullstein), for example, recounts the period of reunification from a child's perspective.

"November 9, 1989, was simply incredible," she told DW. She was 10 years old at the time. When her mother bought her winter boots with the 100 Deutsche Marks she received from the West German state — a welcome gift given to all East German citizens — she was so disappointed that she felt like crying. But later, a friend of her parents' let her buy so many sweets at the supermarket that they lasted until Christmas.

"The disappointment really set in afterwards, with what happened over the course of the following year. It was unbelievable how quickly an entire system was suddenly swept away and a new one built up, as if to say, 'There you go. You're welcome'," Streisand recalled. "I think it was just too fast for people."

The people of East Germany, or the GDR, had brought about the fall of the Berlin Wall themselves through a civil rights movement and numerous demonstrations. For many, however, the goal was not to dissolve the state immediately but to reform it.

Among them was Anke Feuchtenberger, born in 1963 in East Berlin. Her childhood was spent in East Berlin and in the East German region of Western Pomerania, where she now lives again and feels "very much at home."

Today, she teaches at the University of Applied Sciences in Hamburg, meaning she spends time on both sides of the former divide. Feuchtenberger is often described as Germany's most influential comic artist. Her work has also garnered international acclaim.

"Back then, as artists, we tried to bring about a change through posters and flyers — to gain more freedom without immediately abolishing socialism," she explained.

At the time, the fall of the Berlin Wall stirred up mixed feelings in Feuchtenberger: "I soon realized that the creative and revolutionary aspects of our movement were very quickly being smothered by consumerism, and that nationalist tendencies — which had already been noticeable before — were coming to the fore," Feuchtenberger recalled. "That made me afraid."

Meanwhile, for photographic artist Simon Menner, born in 1978 in Emmendingen, in the West German state of Baden-Württemberg, Berlin was very far away. As Menner put it, he experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall as a child in a "rather abstract" way. Today, Berlin is his home.

In his experience, the way films and documentaries portrayed East Germany around the time of reunification was very bleak. "But West Germany in the '80s," he said, "was also bleak and very staid."

This uneven portrayal of the two parts of Germany is an issue that deeply concerns Menner — partly because he unwittingly contributed to it in a small way. Among other things, Menner's work explores the topic of surveillance and how it works.

In the archives of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi — which are freely accessible today as part of the National Archives — he discovered a massive collection of photographs that both fascinated and horrified him and which he wanted to bring to the attention of a wider public.

His photo book "Top Secret" (2012, from publisher Hatje Cantz) features a selection of photos that offer a unique insight into the work of the Stasi. Some are eerie, while others are curious or even absurd.

Menner also tried to look into the photo archive of West Germany's Federal Intelligence Service. "I spent a year trying to gain access — without success," he said.

In hindsight, he now finds his artistic project problematic because he believes it is too one-sided, focusing exclusively on East Germany's past.

According to Menner, West Germany's intelligence services in the 1960s were not exactly models of virtue either, and he believes it is "actually high time" to critically examine this part of history as well. In his view, an honest examination of Germany's past as a whole is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation.

Streisand believes literature can help foster mutual understanding. "Literature opens a window into experiences we haven't had ourselves," she said. "You can immerse yourself in the mind of someone who has had a different life than you have and understand what happened."

Interest in these stories remains strong. In 2023, Feuchtenberger published the nearly 500-page graphic novel "Comrade Cuckoo" (published by Reprodukt), which was the first graphic novel to be nominated for the Leipzig Book Fair Prize in the fiction category.

The story spans a childhood in the fictional East German village of Pritschitanow in the 1960s in the GDR to the post-Reunification era. In it, Feuchtenberger weaves autobiographical memories of her upbringing with fantastical and fictional elements.

The artist said she was surprised "that, so long after the fall of the wall, my stories have sparked such great interest in the West."

In particular, the fact that the main character, Kerstin, rarely sees her parents because they both work full-time is a topic that often comes up at readings. In the GDR, everyone had the right to work, she said. At the same time, it was a civic duty.

Could the West German interest in this stem from the fact that full-time employment for both parents has long been less common in the West? It's possible, said Feuchtenberger.

When looking toward their shared future, the two East German women are more optimistic than Menner, from West Germany.

"In Berlin, I often don't even notice anymore whether I'm in the West or the East," said Menner. "But when it comes to sociopolitical issues, politicians should listen to older and younger people more closely," he added, referring to the recent election successes of far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD . "Otherwise, things are going to get difficult in the near future."

"It's very important to step outside our own bubble because people all over the world are facing problems. Constantly focusing on this German-German divide that has emerged between the groups doesn't help," said Feuchtenberger.

"For me personally, the whole issue of borders has somehow dissolved," she explained. This is due in no small part to the many trips abroad that have taken her to various places around the world.

Moreover, in her hometown near the Polish border, she observes how animals couldn't care less about the border. "They come from the east and the west and do whatever they want," she said. That's why she also gave "Comrade Cuckoo" the working title "A German Animal in a German Forest," "because I found the absurdity of an animal having a nationality so funny."

"This East-West thing — our children won't have any interest in it at all," said Streisand. "Young people don't care where their parents come from. Can I get a job that will support a family? Do I have to go to war? Right now, completely different things are relevant."

This article was originally written in German.

The Celtic great moved south of the border in 1977

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When Kenny Dalglish arrived at Liverpool from Celtic in 1977, he arrived as a 26-year-old, just entering his peak years.

Signed as a replacement for Hamburg-bound Kop icon Kevin Keegan, Dalglish eclipsed even King Kev’s achievements in Reds shirt over the next decade and a half.

But the Scot’s move to Anfield almost happened a decade earlier, when he was still a teenager.

“Myself and another boy were invited for trials with Liverpool when I was a teenager,” Dalglish tells FourFourTwo. “We played a game, then I was asked to go back for a couple of weeks.

“Shanks [Billy Shankly] was there, I played a game and they said. ‘We'd like to sign you.' I thought, ‘It's a bit far from Glasgow…' I knew that Liverpool was a great club, I just thought it was too far away for a 15-year-old boy going down there by himself.”

Dalglish would go on to become a Celtic great, winning four Scottish league titles and four Scottish Cups before Liverpool came knocking again.

“Then in 1977, when I was 26, I'd been in South America for World Cup warm-ups with Scotland, because the World Cup was going to be in Argentina the next year,” he recalls.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I came home, Celtic were going to Australia and I said to the manager, ‘I don't want to go.' Jock Stein said, ‘Go home and think about it.'

“I told him, ‘I have thought about it', and by the way, for me to stand up to him like that, I was terrified! I stayed at Celtic Park and trained with the reserves.

What followed next was a clear sign that Stein was preparing for life without his star player.

“When the first team came back, I played a couple of pre-season games, one at Dunfermline. We were in the dressing room, ready to go out and I was captain, but Big Jock threw the ball at one of the other players and said, ‘On you go, you take them out.'

“The rest of them were all saying to me, ‘Oh… where are *you* going?' I said, ‘I don't know!' “After the game, I dropped into my father-in-law's pub on the way home. Big Jock phoned the pub and said, ‘Right, do you still want to go?' I said, ‘Aye, boss.' He said, ‘Get yourself up here, there are two people who want to talk to you.'

“It was about 10.30pm – Bob Paisley and the chairman of Liverpool were there. About five minutes later, everything was agreed.”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#950. Raheem Sterling avoids jail for £270,000 Lamborghini crash: England star handed suspended prison sentence after telling court he underwent 12-day rehab stint for laughing gas 'problem'

Published: 04:50 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 14:13 EST, 25 November 2026

Former England football star Raheem Sterling avoided prison for dangerous driving and possession of nitrous oxide after it was revealed he spent 12 days in rehab.

The 31-year-old was handed a 12-month sentence, suspended for 18 months, at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court today and has been banned from driving for two years.

He was also ordered to complete 100 hours of community service and must pay a victim surcharge of £187 as well as prosecution costs of £85.

Sterling – who is currently without a club but has played for Liverpool, Manchester City and Chelsea – pleaded guilty after crashing his £270,000 Lamborghini Urus SUV on May 28 while under the influence of laughing gas.

Four police forces received reports about the footballer's dangerous driving before he eventually crashed his car into a metal gate on the A327 in Hampshire during rush hour on the morning of May 28.

Sterling told police he had 'a problem' with laughing gas after subjecting rush hour motorists to a terrifying 90 minutes of dangerous driving, in which he zig-zagged on the M3 and M25 motorways before swerving onto a slip road and crashing into a metal gate. Police found six canisters of nitrous oxide in his car.

Raheem Sterling is pictured leaving Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Wednesday, shaking hands with his solicitor Leo Martin - he avoided prison time

Sterling is seen after being pulled over by police earlier this year while under the influence of laughing gas in his Lamborghini - he later spent 12 days in rehab

In the police station, Sterling was asked to judge 30 seconds with his eyes closed but was so impaired that he recorded 52.

The footballer – who wore trainers, a black quarter-zip jumper with a white t-shirt and black trousers – froze as he waited for the judge to enter the court room.

He sat with his back against the wall in the glass dock and kept eye contact with her while she read her sentencing remarks.

District Judge Kirsty Allman revealed that Sterling sought addiction treatment on June 15 and went into rehab for 12 days.

She explained that nitrous oxide had 'become a maladaptive coping mechanism during a difficult period in his career', adding that he was a 'role model'.

While his sentence does not mandate therapeutic intervention, the lead therapist at Banbury Lodge – where Sterling checked in – feels further treatment would be 'beneficial'.

His MBE, charitable work and time spent in rehabilitation were cited as mitigating factors, helping him avoid a prison sentence.

Allman added: 'You are 31 years old and a man of previous good character. I accept your character has been positively exemplary.

Sterling leaves the court with his solicitor having been given a suspended sentence

Image issued by the Crown Prosecution Service shows the damage to the Lamborghini Urus being driven by Sterling

'(But) these offences are so serious that neither a fine nor a community order can be justified. The custodial threshold is clearly crossed, and custody is unavoidable.'

However, custody was avoided because the law was changed in March 2026, with custodial sentences of one year or less presumed to be suspended – unless there are specific aggravating features – because of the overcrowded prison population.

Temporary chief inspector Chris Sharland of Hampshire Police said: 'Nitrous oxide, commonly known as laughing gas or NOS, is a Class C drug, and driving whilst under its influence is an emerging threat to the safety of motorists on our roads.

'Driving whilst impaired with nitrous oxide can cause unconsciousness, and in the worst-case scenarios neurological damage or death, so there is a very real risk of causing serious harm to yourself or other motorists.

'We urge drivers to be aware of not only the law, but the risk this type of behaviour carries – one decision can have devastating consequences.'

In his pre-sentencing remarks, Sterling's lawyer, Jason Bartfeld KC, said Sterling is 'more concerned not by damage to his reputation' but the 'consequences' it has had for his family, particularly his children.

He added: 'Mr Sterling recognised the various unhealthy coping mechanisms that brought him to this position and has sought to address these in the most positive and effective way and with some success.

'All of it makes it extremely sad and a matter of his own personal regret, tarnishing his own personal reputation.

'The end point of this is that he is absolutely determined that he will never appear before a criminal court again.'

Police bodycam footage showed the moment that Sterling was arrested with canisters and a deflated balloon on his lap.

An officer could be heard saying 'you can put that down' to the footballer after opening his car door.

He could then be seen taking the items from his lap and putting them behind his seat.

Sterling gets back in the car after his sentencing and is banned from driving for two years

Sterling, who won the PFA Young Player of the Year award in 2018-19, was then read his rights while being arrested after being asked to put his arms behind his back.

There was a 40mph speed restriction on the M25 as he veered from lane to lane during peak travel time, with one witness fearing a ‘fatal collision’.

His arrest, near the Minley interchange, where the A327 meets the M3 in Hampshire, happened four weeks after he had returned to the UK following the end of an abortive attempt to revive his career at Dutch club Feyenoord.

Sterling, from Berkshire, pleaded guilty in September to dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen after a single vehicle collision at 8.45am on May 28.

During that hearing, Basingstoke Magistrates' Court heard that Sterling was so impaired by the laughing gas that he was unable to perform basic police station tests like placing his finger on his nose or placing one foot in front of another.

Barrister Simon Jones, prosecuting, said of Sterling: 'He appeared to be quiet, withdrawn and lethargic and actively fidgeting.

'Eye lids drooping consistent with fatigue or drug impairment. He said he was feeling very cold, despite this being in the middle of a heatwave with 33-degree temperatures.'

The 31-year-old was charged with dangerous driving and possession of laughing gas after swerving his car on the M25 and M3

Motorist Fiona Jennings told police she had looked across to witness the driver of the Lamborghini with a balloon in front of his face which was so big she thought it was an air bag.

It was so big that 'she had no idea how the driver would have been able to see the road ahead,' Mr Jones said.

Ms Jennings described Sterling's driving as 'absolutely horrendous' and expressed 'genuine concern that the driver may kill someone'.

Evidence previously presented to court suggested Sterling was also inhaling laughing gas while at the wheel of the Lamborghini a full seven hours before his arrest.

A concerned witness called police after seeing the driver of the same car entering a McDonalds car park alarmingly fast at 1.10am the same morning and seeing the driver holding up 'a pink, inflated balloon'.

By 7.45am that morning, another motorist concerned by the Lamborghini erratically changing lanes saw the driver placing a white balloon to his mouth and inhaling its contents.

For 30 minutes, that motorist watched the vehicle weave between the inside and outside lanes and come close to smashing into the central reservation.

#949. Norway's ice hockey team says Russia replacing it at World Juniors

The wrangling over Russia's return to international ice hockey continues, with Norway saying it has been kicked out of the next major tournament to accommodate Russia. Switzerland has joined a "boycott."

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had said it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision.

The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey."

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. But Swiss Ice Hockey has responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it's far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," said Mark Carney.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) hope that its team could still play in the upcoming tournament. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," said NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days."

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in May.

"We intend to host the world championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

"However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications."

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the issue could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

For a generation of football fans in the UK, Soccer AM was a staple of their Saturday morning routine.

The Sky TV show combined football, comedy and celebrity guests, all with a healthy dose of general chaos.

When TV newcomer and longtime Soccer AM fan Max Rushden landed the co-presenter job alongside Helen Chamberlain in 2008, he was thrown into a world he had never experienced before.

“Getting the job was mad because I'd never done a TV show in my life, and it definitely showed in the first two years,” Rushden tells FourFourTwo.

“But I loved the show – I was a fan of the week in 2000 and watched it religiously until about two or three years before getting the job, so the whole thing was surreal.”

Premier League officials are 'shocked and furious' after the FA overturned Manchester United defender Leny Yoro's red card at Liverpool - despite the competition's own independent panel unanimously backing the dismissal.

Daily Mail Sport understands that the Premier League's Key Match Incidents (KMI) panel has returned a 5-0 verdict in support of referee Sam Barrott's decision to send off Yoro. The panel also backed VAR's decision not to intervene. Their findings will be released next Wednesday.

But an extraordinary row has now erupted, with United celebrating a successful appeal while the Premier League and refereeing body Pro Ref stand by the original decision.

United appealed against the red card following Sunday's 4-0 defeat at Anfield - Mauricio Pochettino's first game in charge - and an independent FA regulatory commission, consisting of three former players, rescinded Yoro's one-match ban on Tuesday.

The Frenchman was sent off for bringing down Alexander Isak as he ran clear on goal in the eighth minute. United disputed the referee's view that the Liverpool striker would have got to the ball before goalkeeper Senne Lammens, having taken a heavy touch.

The FA panel appeared to agree, on the basis Yoro did not deny Isak an obvious goalscoring opportunity, meaning the Frenchman is free to play against Brentford at Old Trafford on Saturday.

Yoro was sent off for this foul on Alexander Isak - but his red card was overturned on Tuesday

Barrott and his on-field officiating team from Sunday are believed to be angry at the overturn

However, top-flight officials are now understood to be demanding answers as to how this has happened, with Pro Ref chief Howard Webb backing his referees.

'That (the red card) was the referee's call, made on the field,' said Webb. 'Then the VAR checks whether the decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect - and formed the opinion it wasn't.

'I think by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball. The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable, I guess. Certainly not clearly wrong.'

United sources have branded this interpretation as 'totally wrong' and say it is a process error that fails to interpret the rules properly. They believe that the VAR audio proves there was no meaningful consideration given to challenging Barrott's decision.

United dispute that it was a subjective call and say that it can be proved objectively in a matter of minutes using data that Isak could not have reached the ball before Lammens, even at top speed.

The Premier League and Pro Ref did not comment.

Gretchen Tessmer is an attorney/writer based in the US/Canadian borderlands of Northern New York.

There’s a bell ringing in the Underground.

The copper-line page phone in Shaft #4 is going off, but it takes a minute for any of the miners to notice. They’re too busy dealing with a tunnel collapse and subsequent break in the geothermal line servicing Sectors 51–57.

It’s late morning, as measured by the water clocks and those who swear by them. It’s midnight, as determined by the Moon and stars, cavorting a few thousand feet above their heads. But the oldest miner on this crew is 60, which is about 30 years too young to remember stars or moons, or appreciate the difference between morning and night.

This is one reason why the Mona Lisa Lottery, so loved by the old-timers, fails to stir up the same excitement it used to. Too intent on repairs, the miners forget that the annual drawing is scheduled for today.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Eventually, the ringing registers and curiosity calls them away from their work. Headlamps bob up and down in the dark. The sound of axes and drills drops off sharply, save for one stubborn miner still working, right below a rock face chiselled with the encouraging-but-long-false words: This Way Out.

They gather round the ringer box and the foreman hushes them before pressing the phone tight to one ear, cupping his free hand over the other. Every noise echoes tenfold in the tunnels, and the foreman has to ask the voice on the other end to repeat themselves.

“Abel?” the foreman repeats. “Are you sure?”

A few miners huff wry laughs at the name, muttering, “Of course it’s him.”

The foreman looks around, failing to find the lucky winner among his workers, “Well, where is he?”

A couple outstretched thumbs and jerks of the head give the foreman his answer, unmistakably directed towards the only pickaxe still singing in the dark.

No one can opt out of the Mona Lisa Lottery. No one can give away their ticket to someone else.

But Abel’s tempted to decline the honour. He’s got work to do. And climbing up 2,000 feet to wait in line with the other winners for hours, all to stare at a square 30-by-21 inches for 5 whole minutes, doesn’t seem like a good use of his time.

It’s only Adèle, the old woman in the cave next door, who convinces him to make the trek upstairs.

Adèle was ten when the evacuations happened. She’s now two months shy of being a proper centenarian. Her mind isn’t as sharp as it used to be. She can’t remember what she had for breakfast, but she remembers the horrors they descended from well enough, all those lines of desperate people sent down below with canned goods, heirloom seeds and not much else.

The treasures preserved from the Old World are few and Abel’s been given the chance to see one of the last. Arguably, the best. If she wasn’t blind as a bat, Adèle might kill him for his ticket. If she didn’t love him like a son, that is.

“Don’t be a fool,” she tells him plainly. “Go see what you’ve been missing.”

The journey to the higher levels snakes up ladders and through tight squeezes, skirting the underbelly of the Safe Zone. There’s a breath of strange breeze up here, not conjured by any air machines. It makes some winners too nervous and they abandon the wait, rushing back down the way they came.

Abel’s not afraid. But he still thinks it’s a waste of time.

Adèle warned him that the wait for the Mona Lisa was just like this. When she was eight, her family waited for two hours just to get a glimpse. It doesn’t make sense to him. He doesn’t understand how a mere painting could be worth the trouble.

He’ll never know. Because that’s not what the Mona Lisa Lottery is all about. Despite the name, Abel’s not queuing for oil paint on a poplar panel.

The Mona Lisa is not in the Underground. They couldn’t waste the limited space. Leonardo’s lady still sits in the crumbling ruins of her museum gallery, her half-smile gone grimmer these days. She’s lonely without visitors. A wild boar passed her way a decade before, searching for truffles in the jungles of the overgrown Louvre. No one’s been by since.

She sighs into her patient smile; she waits with folded hands. Ever the optimist, she thinks her friends may return someday.

#943. Iran war oil shock drives dip in global emissions, study shows

Global carbon emissions are expected to fall slightly in 2026, but not because of major progress on climate action. Instead, it's high energy prices following the US attack on Iran that's driving the trend.

Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a new study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.

"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons."

The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.

The study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.

"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters said. "What we see this year is [that] oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%."

It is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

While the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind the temporary emissions reversal, there has also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

And even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

#942. Man Utd are in relegation trouble and Carrick must be sacked

Michael Carrick stood perfectly still and raised his left arm, and his index finger, high in the air. Around him, chaos. As it had been all afternoon. Substitute Patrick Dorgu had just headed in a corner to rescue a point for Manchester United in the 96th minute and, maybe, save Carrick his job.

Going into added time and United were two goals behind. It seemed all was lost for them against Aston Villa and for their head coach, but how telling was the reaction, in the directors’ box, of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, who both jumped up in celebration? They were far more animated than Carrick and could not contain themselves.

"Football is a contact sport!" 🗣️ Did Senne Lammens foul Zion Suzuki for Man United's equaliser? 🤔 https://t.co/KCb1lHqPHP

Did their behaviour betray not just their excitement in the moment but their relief at not having to sack Carrick during this forthcoming international break? If so, they need to think again. They need to make a sober and rational decision based on evidence. And the evidence shows that Carrick must go. Because this kind of football is unsustainable. This kind of football does not work. This kind of football is stupid.

United are 18th in the Premier League. They have won one game in 10 in the league. They have conceded 15 goals in their last five matches in the league and Champions League. When they play Liverpool away, their next game, on November 22, it will be the first time they have done so from inside the relegation zone since March 1937.

They appear shockingly disorganised. Tactics seem to be an after-thought, their motivation is lacking until desperation kicks in. United conceded two goals within four minutes at the start of the game. And then two more within eight minutes of the second half kicking off.

The bottom line is this: can they afford not to make a change? If they do not, United could be accused of copping out and gambling with their status. So, Berrada and Wilcox must ask: what is Carrick doing in the dressing room and on the training ground? What messages are he and his assistant Steve Holland sending out? Are the players even listening?

At the end the fans sang Carrick’s name after United became the first team in the Premier League to come back twice from being two goals down. That also summed up the fog of confusion at a club who so obviously lack direction – from the top down – and need to get a grip of themselves. Carrick talked about having to “tighten up” the defending. But everything needs to be stronger. More taut. More competitive.

Chaos can be entertaining. Chaos can be fun. As an advert for the Premier League this was outstanding. United fans will be thrilled with the Fergie-time comeback. But chaos is also unsustainable. No one knows what to expect from United.

In the cold light of day Villa manager Unai Emery will have to ask himself whether he, too, got it wrong. His substitutions did not work, bizarrely taking off too much experience, such as his outstanding captain John McGinn, and he handed United a late initiative when it looked like all hope was lost.

But analyse the goals that United conceded. Any rational response would suggest a change should be made. Take the first two. Villa scored with their first attack, moving the ball from a throw-in, with zero pressure on them, from left to right with McGinn finding Alysson. The winger’s low first-time shot went through the legs of goalkeeper Senne Lammens, who had an awful game. Lammens’s only positive contribution was to come up for the late corner from which Dorgu scored, possibly getting away with a sly nudge on Villa’s Zion Suzuki.

What a start for Aston Villa! 🔥 Alysson fires home to give the the visitors the lead https://t.co/F0nfSRMWRa

Then Lammens conceded a second as he fumbled a shot from Alysson, after the Brazilian was again teed up by McGinn with Nicolas Jackson tucking home the rebound. It followed a poor defensive header from Leny Yoro. It would not be his last one.

Nicolas Jackson has made it 2-0 to Aston Villa after just 4 minutes and boos ring out around Old Trafford 🤯 https://t.co/G7oWDNMjGS

At that point, even so early, it felt over. For United. For Carrick. Then it got complicated. In fairness, United responded brilliantly. By half-time it was 2-2 and a potentially mutinous situation, with the fans on edge and unfurling new banners attacking the hierarchy – including one which read “your funeral not ours” – had turned and were raucous in a positive way.

Matheus Cunha, with a sharp turn and run into the Villa penalty area before being brought down, earned the spot kick from which Bruno Fernandes pulled back the first goal. Former Villa midfielder Youri Tielemans drew them level with a first-time shot. Not just that but they peppered the Villa goal.

Youri Tielemans against his former club! 😱 Manchester United are level just before the break! https://t.co/8kFOQkl814

Then they conceded two more in quick succession with a ridiculous trip on Alysson by Diogo Dalot, who was given the runaround at left-back until he was substituted to cheers. McGinn scored from the penalty. It was 4-2 when Yoro inexplicably headed a McGinn free-kick goalwards, Lammens tipped it on to the crossbar and Leon Goretzka eventually bundled the ball in.

Tellingly, the United supporters appeared too stunned to protest. The game meandered to what felt like an inevitable conclusion, petering out much like, surely, Carrick’s time in charge.

But, football, bloody hell. As someone – who was appointed United manager 40 years ago last week – once said. Dorgu made a difference. As did Joshua Zirkzee, another substitute, as the pair became United’s unlikely saviours, the striker sweeping home the full-back’s cross in the 92nd minute, with six added on.

Then a corner was won. The roar went up – as did Lammens. But it was Dorgu who met the delivery from close range to salvage a point. But the big question is: did he also salvage Carrick?

Michael Carrick has insisted he remains the right man to lead Manchester United and will not walk away despite the club being marooned in the relegation zone.

United came from 2-0 and 4-2 down to claim a last-gasp 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on another wild day at Old Trafford.It means United still only have one Premier League win to their name this season and are languishing in 18th position, a point adrift of safety, heading into the international break when the Old Trafford hierarchy must decide whether to keep faith with Carrick or appoint their third manager this year.

Carrick cut a spiky figure when asked about his future by Sky Sports and whether he would walk away.

“That’s not going to happen,” Carrick said, before asking “will there?” when it was put to him that there would “clearly” be conversations about his future.

“We haven’t won enough games, but I expect to move forward and keep working on the things we’ve been working on and showing a lot of good in the game today,” he said. “Tighten up on some things and start winning football matches.”

"That's not going to happen" 🗣️ Michael Carrick responds to the notion that he could resign as Manchester United head coach 🔴 https://t.co/q1fBKSXL7l

Roy Keane, the former United captain, likened Carrick to a “politician”. “It’s hard to believe what’s coming out of the United camp because we can’t even be sure they’re being honest with themselves. Villa enjoying a strong spell of possession in United’s half now, Mbaye proving an outlet down the left since coming on as a substitute.

Goretzka with a really poor square pass inside his own half, and Kamara cannot make a challenge against Cunha, but his shot from a tight angle is straight at Suzuki. Fernandes then lifts a cross over the bar.

Emery’s turn to make changes: McGinn and Alysson off, Barkley and Hemmings on.

Mbeumo shoots just wide of the far post from 20 yards out, not a bad effort. Villa are not impregnable, but they are managing this half’s two-goal lead better than the first. A touch more compact, and winning fouls to halt any nascent United momentum.

Triple sub by United: Dalot, Amad and Tielemans the players off, replaced by Dorgu, Lacey and Mount. Hearty cheers from Lacey from the United fans, the young attacker who set up Cunha’s winner against Roma.

Huge cheers when Dalot is substituted from the United fans followed by boos as he left the pitch. Shades of Zirkzee against Newcastle.

Tielemans slices a left-footed shot over the bar from distance, but both teams are still finding it easy to progress the ball and create half chances. There are surely more goals on the way if it carries on like this.

Attack, or counter-attack, might prove the best form of defence for Villa because Alysson is tearing it up down their right flank. Heaven hacks him down at the expense of a yellow card, and the forward requires some treatment.

Chaotic defending from the free-kick, with Yoro losing his bearings and heading against his own crossbar from a few yards out. There ensues a goal-mouth scramble, but Goretzka was on hand to make sure from a few yards out. United two goals down for the second time in the game. Can they do it all again?

Good work in midfield from McGinn to protect the ball not once but twice and buy a foul from Fernandes, who throws his hands up at the decision. That is the name of the game for Villa: if they can keep the ball for longer spells, chances will open up around the edge of United’s box.

Mazraoui with a misdirected cross that drifts behind for a goal kick. Old Trafford is quiet again, save for the Villa fans in the corner. Maguire has his critics, but his half-time departure has not helped United’s cause. Their defence was flimsy enough with him there.

Just like in the first half, Villa have an early goal. Unerring finish from the spot from McGinn, plenty of power and sending Lammens the wrong way. Can Villa keep their foot on the pedal this time?

It appears enforced, with Harry Maguire replaced by Ayden Heaven. United will play the second half with two 20-year-old central defenders.

United have hope again just when things looked completely hopeless. After Aston Villa scored twice in the opening four minutes, thoughts were turning to official club statements and pictures of corner flags.

Carrick’s team have been irrepressible since though, attacking Villa with abandon and scoring two well-deserved goals.

Villa lost their grip too easily with a two-goal lead, and it’s not the first time you can say that about an Emery team.

VAR have a decision to make after a high boot from Fernandes on Alysson in United’s box but the incident is checked and cleared.

Villa miss a chance to go in with a lead, Alysson on the run again and he dinked the ball over Lammens but wide of the far post.

The midfielder has scored against his former club, a shot from the edge of the box squeezing under Suzuki after a well-placed cut-back from Mazraoui down the right. Mbuemo was stood in front of the goalkeeper, but he was onside and the goal stands.

It looked like United’s chance to draw level before half-time had gone when Amad, without a United goal for almost a year, had a shot from a great position saved but Tielemans has equalised after another good attack. United have responded well since Fernandes’ penalty although Villa very nearly went back ahead with Alysson, who has been a menace down United’s left, almost scoring.

Youri Tielemans against his former club! 😱 Manchester United are level just before the break! https://t.co/8kFOQkl814

Big save from Suzuki to deny Amad! Strong hand from the goalkeeper to keep it out and avoid spilling the ball to a United player.

Suzuki called upon to sweep up well outside of his area, before a Fernandes shot hits Mazraoui in the head. Jackson wastes a Villa counter-attack with a careless pass.

Mazraoui penalised for a foul on Manzambi near the corner of the penalty area. Welcome territory, and the chance to push for a third goal before half-time.

Floated in by McGinn, but Torres’s header loops comfortably over the bar.

Maguire and Yoro defend well against Jackson’s peeling run in the left channel before United come forward again through Cunha. The ball is worked across to Amad, who cuts inside Maatsen a little too easily and shoots not far wide of the far post.

The last few minutes of the game have been quieter, welcome news from Villa’s perspective. Jackson, Alysson and Manzambi still look a threat when they have a chance to attack space from deep, but they need more midfield control from Kamara and Goretzka.

Fernandes whips free-kick wide of the post from a crossing position, but feels he should have a corner for a flick off Suzuki. The Old Trafford crowd are up again after Mainoo slides in to win a tackle in midfield.

This is one-way traffic now, United swarming all over Villa and Amad’s deflected shot trickles just wide of Suzuki’s post. United’s response to the first four minutes of the game has been impressive, but Villa are playing a part in their own downfall.

United on top now and have a little momentum after that shocking start. The crowd have also lifted noticeably.

United are certainly in the ascendancy now, Villa allowing too much space around the edge of their box. From there, a Fernandes shot deflects off the boot of John McGinn and loops not far wide of the post. Suzuki palms the ball behind for another corner.

The goalkeeper clears the second corner in unorthodox fashion, before Mainoo’s shot deflects into Suzuki’s gloves.

Cracking effort from Cunha, going for the far corner from 25 yards with a curling shot but Suzuki was equal to it and tipped the ball around the post. From the resulting corner, Aston Villa’s goalkeeper gathers at the second attempt after attempting to catch.

A more chaotic game suits United, Villa will want some more sustained periods of possession. McGinn and Manzambi’s positioning is causing United problems. Mazraoui is stepping out to mark the Swiss but not always getting there. Diligent defending from Amad to track back against Maatsen.

Some fans had been encouraging a walk-out in the 21st minute (to signal 21 years of “decay” under the Glazers”) but if any fans have left it’s very few. Old Trafford still packed.

Villa trying to restore some order with considered passing from deep, but Maguire steps in well to take the ball off McGinn. Mbemo is the flagged for offside. United are the team with bigger problems, but Villa do not look wholly trustworthy themselves.

The slow, stuttered run up pays off this time as Fernandes waits for Suzuki to dive right, before passing the ball the other way. Game on.

A lifeline for Man Utd! 🔥 Bruno Fernandes converts from the penalty spot to reduce the defecit! https://t.co/wy7L1iAhbx

Kamara penalised for lunging at Cunha in the penalty from the wrong side, and his left leg caught the United man before he got to the ball. Not particularly contentions, but VAR is taking time to check. Decision confirmed.

Manzambi has enjoyed an impressive start to his Villa career, as well as this game. When there is space for him to stride into, United’s midfield appears incapable of stopping him.

Lindelof clears Cunha’s cross. “You should have signed for a big club!” is the chant from Villa’s away end, aimed at Youri Tielemans.

Then Manzambi releases Jackson into space, Villa’s centre-forward galloping into space but Yoro did well to slow him down and avoid pulling a shirt at the expense of a corner.

Fernandes then drags a snap shot wide of the post. Frantic stuff.

2 - After three minutes and 40 seconds, this is the earliest Manchester United have ever been 2-0 down in a Premier League game. Slumber. https://t.co/76iMwVLhTK

Villa continue to pour forward with menace, United’s defence offering all the resistance of wet tissue paper. I’m not sure I can recall a home team starting a match this badly, perhaps Spurs vs Fulham last season runs it close.

The sheer scale of the incompetence is staggering. Two goals down in three minutes and 40 seconds, shambolic defending all round, dismal goalkeeping, boos echoing around after that second Villa goes in, the ownership targeted at every opportunity. “You’re getting sacked in the morning” the Villa fans sing at Michael Carrick. And now “Unai’s right, you’re f------ s----”, a nod to Emery being heavily linked with the Old Trafford job but close to signing a new deal with Villa. Tielemans is being taunted with chants of “You used to play for a big club” and “you sold your soul for this s---hole”.

These scenes are truly surreal, Manchester United are 2-0 down inside four minutes. This is a new low.

It was a meat and drink free-kick floated into the box, the ball dropped for Alysson to hit from the edge of the box, and Lammens could only parry back into danger.

Jackson was free as a bird to score from a few yards, and he was well onside.

Nicolas Jackson has made it 2-0 to Aston Villa after just 4 minutes and boos ring out around Old Trafford 🤯 https://t.co/G7oWDNMjGS

United’s fans and Jason Wilcox in the stands look dumbstruck, it is the worst possible start.

Bright play from Villa who are first to every ball, working the ball with sharpness across the box from right to left, and Alysson takes his shot first time and it creeps under the body of Lammens.

What a start for Aston Villa! 🔥 Alysson fires home to give the the visitors the lead https://t.co/F0nfSRMWRa

Villa get the game under way, and they have turned United around. The home team will kick towards the Stretford End in the first half.

Green and gold balloons galore on the Stretford End. Remembrance Sunday will be marked before kick-off with the Last Post and a minute’s silence.

United fans have paraded a new banner in the Stretford End that reads: “We don’t want a new stadium, we want new owners.” Hundreds of green and gold balloons are again being released – a nod to the club’s original colours and a symbol of protest. Lots of anti Glazer and Sir Jim Ratcliffe chants again reverberating with the co-owners told to: “Sell United and f--- off home”.

It’s not the only banner. One reads: “History, Dignity, Integrity, You Stole It All”. Another read “Jim Ain’t The One”. One simply says: “Sell Up.”

"We don't want a new stadium, we want new owners" #MUFC #AVFC https://t.co/6maQckC0qm

Taylor Harwood-Bellis starts at the back for Villa, and his father-in-law Roy Keane is in the Sky Sports studio.

They will kick-off in 19th, two points adrift of safety. Sunderland’s win over Chelsea lifts them above United, but Palace are now bottom after a 3-1 home defeat by Liverpool.

This “Glazers Out, Ratcliffe Out” flag is being passed around on the forecourt outside Old Trafford.

One fan group is calling for supporters to walk out in the 21st minute in protest at 21 years of Glazer ownership.

Once upon a time, the only Old Trafford flyers on the agenda were Ryan Giggs and Andrei Kanchelskis. Not so today.

Unai Emery has picked a surprising back four, it could end up being a situational back three of Lindelof, Harwood-Bellis and Torres when Maatsen raids forward from left-back. Villa fans are keen to see more of Mbaye, their summer signing from PSG, but he has to settle for a place on the bench.

With Lisandro Martinez suspended, Yoro moves inside from right-back to partner Maguire. Dalot annd Mazraoui can play full-back on both sides. There is a lack of legs and steel in that midfield, and Villa are one of the most adept teams at playing through the middle of the pitch into the likes of McGinn and Manzambi in the pockets.

United starting XI: Lammens, Dalot, Maguire, Yoro, Mazraoui, Tielemans, Mainoo, Fernandes, Amad, Mbeumo, Cunha

United's starting XI to face Aston Villa 🔴📋 ➡️ Youri Tielemans and Nous Mazraoui ⬅️ Carlos Baleba and Ayden Heaven 💪 @PatrickDorgu13 returns to the bench https://t.co/w24eW6tO2b

With four Premier League games in progress the picture is ever-changing, but United are currently 19th in the Premier League table. The club, famously, were relegated in 1974 with the coup de grâce applied by Denis Law’s backheel when the Scot was playing in a City shirt. In this piece, James Ducker looks back on the previous occasions when one of the world’s biggest clubs has flirted with calamity.

When Villa dropped into the Championship, it did not change the fact they were the biggest club in the Midlands. No matter what Tom Brady does at Birmingham City, that’s not changing any time soon. They sought and achieved promotion by raiding Brentford.

Nobody was complaining about a sleeping giant taking Dean Smith, Ezri Konsa or Ollie Watkins and potentially stalling Brentford’s progression.

Nor was it suggested hiring Emery from Villarreal was an odd move given that the Spanish side had recently won the Europa League and reached the latter stages of the Champions League.

Michael Carrick says he has been given no assurances about his future beyond this afternoon’s crucial game against Aston Villa at Old Trafford.United are searching for only their second Premier League win of the season and first in 70 days after the club’s worst start to a campaign for 40 years piled the pressure on Carrick.They dropped into the relegation zone last night following Nottingham Forest’s victory over Manchester City and will be bottom by the end of the weekend if they lose to Villa and Crystal Palace and Sunderland both win.The Old Trafford hierarchy opted to give Carrick more time to try to turn their season around following a 3-0 hammering by Bournemouth and 4-1 drubbing in Como, since when United have been beaten 2-0 by Chelsea and recovered from two goals down to overcome Roma 3-2 in the Champions League on Tuesday night.Asked if he had been told outright he would still be in charge next week, Carrick said: “No - no. Just carry on as absolute normal.”Pressed on when he felt his future was uncertain, the head coach added: “No, no. Whatever happens and what’s going to happen is going to happen in terms of the game, we’ve got to prepare right.“I’m really looking forward to playing at home on the back of the other night. The supporters are hopefully looking forward to coming and energised and feeling good about what they might see and we’ve got to repay that.”Another defeat would leave the United board with a big decision to make around Carrick’s future at a time when they are under severe attack from the fanbase.United’s game against Roma was briefly interrupted when tennis balls were thrown on to the pitch in the first half of a game notable for more furious protests against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe.Three people were arrested by Greater Manchester Police for throwing items on to the pitch and are understood to have been hit with automatic three-year football banning orders as a consequence. More in-stadium demonstrations are expected today with regular match going fans encouraged not to buy alcohol or drinks inside Old Trafford and again release green and gold balloons before kick-off.Green and gold were the club’s original colours as Newton Heath and have become a symbol of protest against the ownership. Asked why there had been such a big drop-off from last season, Carrick added: “It’s just inconsistency, that’s within games,” he said.“It can be a number of things, it’s never just one thing: a bit of decision-making, a bit of concentration, things going against us in certain points, sometimes we haven’t helped ourselves. So there’s no excuses for it, it is what it is. The great thing is we can do something about it.”

#941. Sporting Lisbon vs Manchester United: Bruno Fernandes levels from the spot, Liverpool lead at Club Brugge

By HARRY BAMFORTH, LIVE SPORTS COVERAGE REPORTER and LUKE POWER, SPORTS REPORTER

Follow Daily Mail Sport's live coverage for the latest updates from Wednesday's Champions League action as Manchester United travel to Sporting Lisbon while Liverpool take on Club Brugge.

What has just happened? I can't believe it and neither can Kaique Pereira...

Bruno Fernandes has turned this game around, but my word, there's luck and then there is that.

Fernandes has a go from distance and his shot hits a huge divot in the box and bounces over Pereira into the net.

I've never ever seen that before at this level.

They are all trying to con the ref at this point because they know how much he loves his whistle.

Joshua Zirkzee goes to ground in the box this time, but for once the referee doesn't point to the spot.

Club Brugge get us going for the second half and decide that the best strategy is just to continually boot the ball into the air. It doesn't work.

Back at his old stomping ground, Bruno Fernandes buries his spot-kick into the bottom corner.

No celebration from the Sporting man; he races straight back to the halfway line.

Yes, I put WATCH in all-caps. You MUST watch it. WATCH NOW.

This referee doesn't half love pointing the spot, and now one finally goes Manchester United's way.

Lisandro Martinez is bundled over in the box and the referee does not hesitate to blow his whistle.

Another half where Manchester United have it all to do, an all-too-familiar story this season.

They need to conjure up something special here to get all three points in this game.

Karen Carney, former Chelsea star, on TNT Sports:

Now, while Manchester United have been on the wrong end of a couple of decisions tonight, but the goal that was scored came from a stonewall spot kick.

Luis Suarez would have been having kittens when stepping up to the spot after missing just minutes earlier.

But he showed what he was made of, burying it into the bottom corner.

You've got to hand it to them, after conceding so many in Europe recently, Liverpool have done well here. Yes, Brugge aren't world-beaters, but Liverpool have kept top scorer Tresoldi as quiet as a mime. There are no chances where Brugge categorically should have scored. Alisson hasn't had to do much at all.

I did say Manchester United wouldn't get a clean sheet, didn't I?

By conceding in that first half, United have now conceded more goals across all competitions than any other team in Europe's top five leagues.

Luis Suarez's penalty was the 35th goal smashed past Senne Lammens this term.

Plenty of food for thought at half-time. Liverpool go in ahead, having had nearly three-quarters of the ball, but Club Brugge have actually had more shots at six compared to five. They're not making much of their possession, the Reds.

#939. Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

More than 2 billion people worldwide suffer from nutrient deficiencies, most of them in the Global South. The health consequences can be devastating.

Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).

The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.

"In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president. "You could have a severe vitamin D deficiency for months before any symptoms appear at all. The same applies for vitamin B12. By the time symptoms appear, such as nerve damage, it's already too late."

A long-term B12 deficiency can damage the spinal cord, leading to numbness in the limbs, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Less common deficiency-related brain damage can cause memory loss and mental health issues.

All B vitamins play an important role in metabolism, blood formation and healthy nerve function.

Vitamins, along with various minerals such as calcium, magnesium, iron, iodine and zinc, are classed as micronutrients. The body needs to source them from food, as it cannot produce them itself. Our bodies also need macronutrients like carbohydrates, carbohydrates, protein and fats that provide us with energy.

If the body consumes less food than it needs to maintain all bodily functions over a prolonged period of time, then this is known as undernutrition. A recent World Food Organization (FAO) report estimates that approximately 645 million people worldwide suffer from chronic undernutrition.

Malnutrition, on the other hand, occurs when we consume enough calories but lack certain macronutrients or micronutrients in our food. This, too, can make one sick over time and even prove fatal. About 2 billion people worldwide suffer from this so-called hidden hunger, most of them in the Global South. That said, even some people in industrialized nations lack important micronutrients in their nutrition.

One study, for instance, found that just under three-quarters of the US population did not meet the recommended daily intake of vitamin D between 2007 and 2010, with more than two-thirds falling short of the recommended amount of vitamin E. And in Germany, about one-third of the population suffered from vitamin D deficiency in 2017, according to the German Nutrition Society. Such deficiency can cause bone, joint and muscle pain. It may also lead to an increased risk of falls and bone fractures.

About one-third of Germans also had an insufficient intake of iodine, a trace element that is indispensable for the production of thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can therefore disrupt normal thyroid function. Not only that — during pregnancy, a baby's brain and nervous system can only properly develop with an adequate supply of iodine.

The cultivation of agricultural produce with partially long shelf life or high yields has in some cases caused a decrease in the micronutrient content of fruits, vegetables and grains. Whether this drop in micronutrients is impacting human health, however, is a matter of debate.

Malnutrition can result from an unbalanced diet that, while filling and providing energy, lacks essential micronutrients. Examples of such empty calories include fast food and highly processed foods, as well as white bread and white rice.

Poverty is often the reason for such an unbalanced diet, for example when people in the Global South can only afford to buy staples such as flour or rice.

Another study found that in Germany, households at risk of poverty are more likely to consume foods that are low in nutrients and high in calories.

Depression is also associated with an increased risk of nutrient deficiency. "People often lose their appetite, and when they neglect their self-care, they may end up eating a very unbalanced diet," Pirlich told DW. His research shows that older adults and people who live alone often develop malnutrition, too. The risk also increases the more medications a person takes.

Many diseases result in the body being less efficient at absorbing or utilizing nutrients through the intestines. This applies to people with inflammatory or chronic disease, such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, liver disease and cancer.

The DGEM estimates that some 30% of all patients receiving inpatient care in Germany are affected by or at risk of malnutrition. Yet health insurance data shows that only about 1% of patients are screened and treated for nutrient deficiencies.

Often, patients' malnutrition worsens during their hospital stay. The consequences can be serious, potentially causing additional complications, delayed recuperation, longer hospital stays and even increased mortality rates. This results in higher healthcare expenditure, amounting to billions each year.

German policymakers and medical associations are therefore developing a plan to better screen for and treat malnutrition in hospitals. The road map will be ready by 2027 and copy the Dutch approach in the sense that all patients are checked for nutritional deficiencies upon hospital admission.

Pirlich wants to see such screenings for at-risk groups in outpatient clinics, too: "This includes all those with chronic and serious illnesses and, above all, older adults."

To prevent poverty-related malnutrition, Pirlich suggests increased access to healthy food, offering free school meals as an example.

The nutritional expert recommends eating a diet that is varied and largely plant-based. "Secondary plant compounds have a very positive effect, and if you eat a highly diverse diet, you consume many different foods that are [nutritionally] beneficial," said Pirlich.

There's a simple rule of thumb: The more colorful your food, the better.

Also, cook vegetables as gently as possible, because overheating and keeping them warm for too long destroys their vitamins. Long storage periods also lead to vitamin loss, so it makes sense to go for seasonal and regional foods in particular.

But even when ensuring a healthy and balanced diet, some people still develop a nutrient deficiency. A blood test can provide clarity, and dietary supplements may help make up for the deficiency.

This article was originally written in German.

Bruno Guimaraes’ return to St James’ Park in Arsenal colours was meant to rub salt into the wounds of Newcastle’s summer exodus, but it galvanised the Magpies who channeled the emotion into a second-half comeback.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It was, for many, the moment Newcastle United ceased to be a force in English football. Bruno Guimaraes’ move to Arsenal was traumatic, and from the club are yet to fully recover.

He was the best player, the talisman, the captain and the one big hope. Without him, an entirely new identity needs to be forged. But Newcastle, and new manager Matthias Jaissle have floundered ever since they parted ways.

Arsenal’s trip north was always going to be about one man. Guimaraes hasn’t been universally derided by Newcastle fans in the way Alexander Isak was, and was made clear by a low key, if still frosty reception when he stepped off the team bus. It was more pantomime than persona non grata.

His exit arguably cut deeper than Isak’s, and those of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali earlier in the summer, but has polarised the fanbase.

For some, his service in leading Newcastle to their first domestic trophy cements his legacy regardless of how ill-timed and controversial his departure was. With so much change at the club going on around him, compounded by the resignation of Eddie Howe in late July, it became clear Guimaraes’ ambitions would no longer be realised on Tyneside.

Seeing Isak, Tonali and Gordon leave with a chance of winning trophies, doubling their wages or both will have stung for the Brazilian. When he arrived in January 2022, he genuinely believed Newcastle would be able to win the Champions League.

Suddenly, they were proudly and publicly embracing a trading model in the transfer market, ripping up their previous approach and starting again. Guimaraes was still central to their plans, but at 28 years of age (now 29), he could no longer wait for phase two of the Newcastle project, especially when promises from phase one remained unfulfilled.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

But over the last four years, he went above and beyond other imports when it came to building a relationship with supporters, talking openly about being an adopted Geordie and wanting to emulate Alan Shearer in becoming a lasting hero.

It was that strength of feeling which Newcastle hoped would coax him into staying another season and led to supporters truly believing in loyalty. But in their time of need, the captain abandoned ship. He was well within his rights to depart, and it is hard to criticise given Arsenal already look like Premier League champions elect.

Yet, having talked up his love for life at Newcastle in the build up, reaffirming how difficult it was to leave, he couldn’t have complained when he was cast in the role of villain.

If his afternoon was summed up in one moment, though, it was his former midfield protege at Newcastle, tapping him on the back as Harvey Barnes swept home a second half equaliser.

Malick Thiaw went on to put the home side in front, only for Noni Madueke to restore parity once again. It was a slow burn, but ultimately, Guimaraes’ presence united Newcastle on the pitch and in the stands.

The expectation was it would be instant and Arsenal would be under siege from a black and white storm whipped up by anger in his direction. Instead, in the first half, it was tame, and when Eberechi Eze opened the scoring, it felt like game over already.

There have been reports in recent weeks suggesting the players do not understand Jaissle’s methods. It certainly felt like that at times; Lukas Hornicek, required to confidently play out from the back, looked shaken every time he had the ball at his feet.

Joe Willock was seen asking questions on his role more than once; Jaissle looked on full of exasperation but, it seemed, with very few answers. A third meek home defeat in succession seemed a formality. Once the game restarted, though, everything shifted.

Jaissle, to his credit, made bold choices, bringing off the one bright spark in the first half, Sean Steur and replacing him with Jacob Ramsey. Tino Livramento and Anthony Elanga were also introduced and Newcastle came alive.

The power, the drive and the ferocity of St James’ Park spurred them on. Suddenly, Jaissle’s approach seemed clear; there was something tangible to build from, a blueprint.

“Everything started with the press,” Thiaw said after the game. “If you win the ball high and early, there is space to attack vertically and directly. It is about how you work off the ball.

“The manager kept it really calm at half time, he knew what we had to do and made good changes. When you are a squad, everybody has to be ready. We used [the crowd’s reaction to Guimaraes] as fuel and we felt that on the pitch.”

Thiaw is one of the players who has stepped into what Jaissle called a “leadership vacuum” in the squad after Guimaraes left. He insists the squad is still backing their manager.

“There are always noises in football, especially outside of the locker room,” he added. “We know what we have to do and what we have to deliver. We are giving everything for the club and the manager.

“If we don’t believe, who will? We will keep improving and we need them. We are all in this together.”

Starting with Arsenal, there is a run of four very tough and potentially season-defining games for Jaissle and Newcastle. Brighton follows, before two home games in a week against Manchester United and Sunderland. It is still far from perfect, but green shoots of optimism may just be emerging.

Ali Dia has gone down in folklore for his absolutely bizarre appearance for Southampton in 1996

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We probably don't need to recap the story, do we? But just in case...

It was 30 years ago exactly, back on 23 November, 1996, when Ali Dia made perhaps the most notorious appearance in the history of Premier League football.

Dia had purported to be the cousin of George Weah to get himself a trial at Graeme Souness' Southampton, and incredibly ended up coming on in place of the injured Matt Le Tissier, only to later be subbed back off hauled back off in the 85th minute of a 2-0 defeat to Leeds.

Dia looked like he'd struggle to play in a Sunday league team, never mind a top-flight outfit - but as Souness explained to FourFourTwo: "That was portrayed like we'd been conned, but no-one was conned.

"Someone phoned up pretending to be George Weah, but we were getting players in every month to come on trial, because we had no money – that's where we got Eyal Berkovic." (Wonder who Berkovic's agent pretended to be?)

"When we got the call about Dia, I said, 'Get him in'.

"Within the first five minutes of a small-sided game at training, I realised he wasn't good enough for us.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"But we didn't have enough players for training sessions, so we said, 'We'll keep him until the end of the week, then we'll tell him'.

"That week we got more and more injuries, to the point where my coach Terry Cooper said, 'We're going to have to have that clown on the bench'.

"I said, 'We can't'. He said, 'We haven't got any players'.

"He was on the bench against Leeds, then Matt Le Tissier comes off injured and I've got a choice between a centre-half, a full-back or a defensive midfielder [or Dia].

"I said, 'Stick Dia on, he'll run about, hopefully occupy their back four'.

"He did that, but he was out of his depth."
