#923. Megaspeed and the battle to go high-end Nvidia chips into China

Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy has shone a light on Megaspeed, the company she worked for. It is under investigation in the US for smuggling Nvidia chips into China, which it denies.

As Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, grapples with CEO Jensen Huang's romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, attention is turning to the much smaller company she worked for.

Alice H., the alleged spy, worked as an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center and AI computing company. It manages data center access, including for some major Chinese tech firms such as Alibaba.

According to Megaspeed's website as of November 2026, the company advertises itself as an "Nvidia cloud partner", saying it provides "computing power product services covering Nvidia's entire GPU product line." GPU stands for Graphic Processing Unit, a specialized electronic circuit that are in high demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, because they are designed to handle high numbers of parallel mathematical calculations. Megaspeed says it provides access for clients to Nvidia's advanced GB200 NVL72 ​computing system.

This type of firm is often referred to as a "neocloud". It buys Nvidia chips and computing power and then rents it out — in this case, at multiple sites across south-east Asia, to different companies. The US has set up strict export controls to prevent that Nvidia's high-performance chips end up in China, because it sees China as a competitor in the global AI race. It also does not want data centers made up of Nvidia chips to be owned by Chinese companies. It does, however, tolerate that data center compute with Nvidia chips be rented out to Chinese companies like Alibaba, and occasionally allows the export of Nvidia chips for specific purposes.

Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia's products in recent years and has been accused of breaching US export controls to divert Nvidia chips into China.

In December 2025, Bloomberg reported that the "once-obscure" Megaspeed had become the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in all of south-east Asia and that the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether or not it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

At the same time, Singapore police began an investigation into whether or not Megaspeed had "violated local laws" without specifying which ones. Those investigations are believed to be still ongoing.

On December 23, 2025, Megaspeed strenuously denied any wrongdoing in a statement — which still appears as the first page for visitors to the company's website as of November 2026.

"There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company," it said. "We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct."

The US government investigation began in 2024. The Commerce Department initially began looking into Megaspeed, but the US Justice Department has since taken over. According to the New York Times, this switch came about after an Nvidia executive directly contacted the Commerce Department about the investigation.

Megaspeed was founded in 2015 and was originally called 7Road International. It changed its name to Megaspeed in March 2023. It is owned by the Singapore-registered Swiftdata, which was set up in October 2023.

Its rise in prominence coincided with a sharp increase in assets, which increased from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024.

Alice H., the woman accused of being a Chinese spy, had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. She is widely seen as an influential figurehead at Megaspeed. She also served as the company's managing director of Megaspeed for eight months in 2023.

The Financial Times reported on Monday that Alice H. leveraged her close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia to pitch AI chips deals to Chinese investors.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The newspaper said that in early 2025, Alice H. sought investment in China for a data center project in south-east Asia, and cited their easy access to Nvidia chips and close relationship with Alibaba.

Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed in June 2024, via subsidiaries. It has remained Megaspeed's largest client, according to reporting by the Financial Times.

In December 2025, Nvidia said its own inquiry into Megaspeed had found no evidence of chips being diverted and that the company was fully owned and operated outside of China, with no Chinese shareholders. The company told Bloomberg at the time that it had visited Megaspeed's facilities on multiple occasions and had seen nothing untoward.

Megaspeed is one of several companies accused of smuggling Nvidia's chips into China or finding ways to give Chinese companies access to them.

Nvidia's high-performance chips are seen as essential for companies looking for the most advanced form of supercomputing to use and develop various AI applications.

Back in 2022, the Biden Administration began severely restricting the sale of the US's most advanced chips to China, part of the two countries' growing rivalry to achieve AI dominance.

However, an illegal smuggling and underground network was soon set up, with many vendors operating to get the chips into China and selling them on to companies there.

In December 2025, US authorities shut down the operations of Hao Global, a US-based shell company with links to China which plead guilty to smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

In June 2026, Taiwanese government agencies raided the offices of Super Micro Computer as part of an investigation into the smuggling of Nvidia chips to China.

While export restrictions have been eased significantly under the Trump administration, there are still significant blocks and restrictions on the most advanced Nvidia chips.

In December 2025, the Trump administration approved several Chinese companies to buy or handle advanced Nvidia H200 chips, a move that sparked significant concern among the US security establishment.

However, that deal has not led to a significant flow of Nvidia chips moving legally to China, amid strict US licencing controls and official reluctance from Beijing to publicly promote Nvidia chips to the detriment of its own alternatives.

#922. England stun world champions Spain in one of their greatest victories

Thomas Tuchel may not have planned it this way, but in one night he gave us all the rich history of the England team at once: some glorious attacking football, some self-sabotage defending, a red card, a late siege and a fight.

This was the beguiling story of Spain 2 England 3, an evening that began with the world champions parading the World Cup trophy and ended with 10 Englishmen defending a lead with their last breath. England beat the world champions in Madrid, and for more than 30 minutes including injury time they did so with 10 men, Dan Burn heading the last ball out as per the tradition of a defensive rearguard action.

This was the game that had it all: including a substitute, in Djed Spence, who had already picked up a yellow card on the bench before he came on. It was a coming-of-age performance in goal for James Trafford. So too for Ben White, the 2022 World Cup departee who scored the third and lunged with astonishing effect in the 84th minute to block a Nico Williams shot.

Trafford again! 👊🏻 An excellent double save from the Leeds United keeper 🙌 https://t.co/L27oQFQO1J

This was a performance good enough to win a World Cup final, never mind Nations League Group A3 – just a shame England neglected to get to that World Cup final in the summer. The fight in question was at half-time as the players came off and White and Fabián Ruiz first tangled and others dived in.

There was so much to admire. England began the night testing Spain’s first-phase passing to breaking point. They began the second half counter-attacking Spain for two goals from Ezri Konsa and White. Then after Elliot Anderson’s red card, this was a different England. With Trafford in inspired form, they held off the relentless Spain for long enough.

Harry Kane scored his 93rd England goal from the spot and was replaced before the end so that Myles Lewis-Skelly’s energy could give the midfield one more lease of life. By the end, the excitement meant that Kane was unable to take his seat on the bench, and he stood alongside Tuchel in the technical area, cajoling and advising.

England have beaten Spain on Spanish territory in recent times, but it was the nature of this performance, its many qualities when the moment required them, that made it so significant. This was the end of a 43-game unbeaten streak for the European and world champions, and it was ended by an England team in their best form in recent years.

Only three who started this game – Kane, Jude Bellingham and Declan Rice – started the final of Euro 2024, lost to Spain. Tuchel’s pool of talent is deeper than it was for his predecessor but there is also a greater maturity to the way they play. The England manager called it the greatest performance of almost two years in charge “given the circumstances… who we play, where we play” and as ever for England just slightly too late.

The defeat by Argentina in the semi-final in Atlanta just stings that little bit more when one considers the craft and resilience England showed on this night. They were under the hammer after Anderson threw an arm over the shoulder of Lamine Yamal and was dismissed before Mikel Oyarzabal converted the penalty that followed. “Thirty minutes against Spain in Spain feels like three hours,” Tuchel said, although Spain had a long way back after the blitzing they took at times in the first hour.

They all had their moments. Anthony Gordon had a strong first half. Morgan Rogers was central to the two goals England scored in the 10 minutes after the break. Anderson demonstrated that he is one of the best midfielders in the world in the hour before his red card. Spain were without Rodri and in his absence his Manchester City successor was in control.

Tuchel encouraged his players to mount a ferocious press against the best first-phase passing team in the world. Brave, but it worked beautifully and for an absorbing opening 10 minutes, Spain looked all at sea. Such was the pressure, the Spain goalkeeper Unai Simón abandoned the usual build-up strategy and launched his goal-kicks to the halfway line.

Even when Spain finally found their rhythm at the mid-point of the first half, England adapted. It took them a while to manage the discomfort of being denied the ball, and the familiar rapid incursions and switches of play. The counter-attacking switch from the early period pressing Spain in their own area yielded the penalty from which Kane scored the first.

Penalty to England! The referee immediately points to the spot after Harry Kane is brought down 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 https://t.co/WIXQcJafki

Anderson snapped into Marc Cucurella and played in Kane with a straight pass punched through the Spain lines. With all his cunning, Kane knew that he could not out-sprint Pau Cubarsi, but he could sucker him into a foul which the England captain did expertly before dispatching the penalty.

WHO ELSE?! 🙌 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Harry Kane converts from the spot just before the break. https://t.co/TY3BjmfaFw

Then in the second half Rogers found space on the right and ran at Cucurella, who was booked after 50 minutes and vulnerable thereafter. It was Rogers’ breakaway down the right, with pace and control that won the corner for the second. Rice’s delivery was on the money and Rogers also managed to step in front of Aymeric Laporte to allow Konsa a free run on to the header.

KONSA!! 🔥 The Arsenal centre-back doubles England's advantage, as the Three Lions lead the world champions 2-0 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿🇪🇸 https://t.co/A0Q6Wwf261

The third England goal was even better. Rogers burst from the right to the inside, breaking through the lines and then via Kane got it back on the left. The ball speared into Bellingham was taken cleanly by the Real Madrid man, who adjusted and picked out the run of White. This goal was his greatest moment in an England shirt.

"This England team are RUNNING RIOT in Spain" 🤩 👀 They lead the World Cup winners by 3-0 in Madrid!! WOW. https://t.co/2GuDnscRb4

It was only another Jarell Quansah error that got Spain back into the game. His mistake allowed Fermin López to play in Yamal for the run in which he was fouled by Anderson for the red card and the subsequent penalty.

Quansah is trying to do the hardest thing asked of a centre-half: play the ball out from the back. His red card in Mexico City and his mistake on Thursday against Croatia have not helped. Nevertheless, John Stones had a tricky start in an England shirt and developed into one of the team’s most important figures.

From another breakaway Yamal crossed for the substitute Williams to score Spain’s second. They would push again but England held on.

Thomas Tuchel praised England’s “statement win” that ended Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run and secured top spot ahead of the world champions in the Nations League.

Tuchel and Declan Rice revealed they had both believed England would end Spain’s long unbeaten streak, and their confidence proved well-founded.

“This was of course a statement victory,” Tuchel said. “I’m happy the players felt so confident. I felt it as well. I also had the same belief [that England would win]. I think we felt it from each other.

“The result followed the performance. I think it was on the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness and it was on the highest level football-wise, in all aspects of the game.”

Tuchel described the nature of England’s win as “the Azteca reloaded” in reference to the World Cup victory over Mexico, but felt the win in Madrid was the best of his reign as head coach.

He said: “Yeah [it was the best performance of his reign so far], given the circumstances and the pressure and the quality and where we played and playing against the reigning world champions. They were unbeaten in 43 games. So putting a performance out there in Madrid, in this environment, that was a very complete performance and the best I’ve had so far.

“The last half an hour felt like Azteca reloaded, to be honest. Again, it was a beautiful week. The commitment to get better is on the highest level.

“I said it many times, I love these players and I love the mentality .We’re building something and that was the next step. It was an amazing atmosphere. I will bottle it up for sure and then unfortunately we have to wait until the quarter-final.”

Thomas Tuchel will speak openly to England’s players about what they should do if they encounter racism in the Nations League Group 3 decider with Spain.

This is the first time England have faced Spain in Madrid since November 2004 when they were beaten 1-0 in the Santiago Bernabéu, a game that was ravaged by obscene chanting. The nations were supposed to play a fixture in the Spanish capital in 2008, but the Football Association insisted it be moved to Seville instead.

Earlier this year, Spanish supporters brought shame on themselves again after a flurry of anti-Muslim chants marred a friendly against Egypt; they were fined $20,000 by Fifa and must play their next friendly in a partially closed stadium.

There will be a full house in the Wanda Metropolitano on Sunday night, as the reigning world and European champions aim to defend their extraordinary unbeaten run of 43 games, and England head coach Tuchel is adamant the atmosphere will be in keeping with the occasion.

The German has, however, made it clear he and his staff will use their platform before the contest to remind England’s players of the steps they should take if the worst scenario unfolds.

Asked about incidents that had pockmarked this fixture before, Tuchel said: “I think I hear it the first time that this happens. I think it’s unacceptable. In any stadium, not even in stadiums, we will never accept racism. We will never be racist towards anyone.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of England’s final Nations League Group 3 decider as Thomas Tuchel’s side take on Spain at Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid.

Although both countries are safely through to the quarter-finals, England will seek revenge on Spain, who beat them in the Euro 2024 final and in their previous Nations League face-off on September 26 at Wembley. That day, Luis de la Fuente’s men profited from Harry Kane’s uncharacteristic penalty miss, England’s general wastefulness in front of goal and some seriously lacklustre defending to earn a chaotic 3-2 comeback victory after falling 2-1 behind at half-time.

Since that defeat, England have won four successive Nations League fixtures against the Czech Republic and Croatia by an aggregate score of 14-1. Last time out, they beat Croatia on Thursday, earning a 2-1 win as Kane, who became England’s most-capped men’s player with 126 appearances, dispatched a second-half penalty to seal the three points. Spearheaded by the Ballon d’Or holder’s brilliance, England must win this evening in order to overtake Spain and top the group.

Speaking ahead of the match, Tuchel said: “I think we are ready to win. Now it’s important that we play with the same mindset that we played at home, and attack them and try to make it a physical game, and try to impose our strength. I think that’s what we want to see. And then you can never predict the result in football, never. But it’s important that we show the mindset that you speak of and the spirit, and we will. I’m very confident about that.”

Meanwhile, fresh from lifting the World Cup in the summer, Spain have a 100% winning record in this season’s Nations League. They currently boast a staggering 43-match unbeaten run in all competitions, since losing a friendly to Colombia back in March 2024. England’s task is daunting, but not impossible.

#921. Aston Villa’s winless run continues with damaging Champions League defeat at Galatasaray

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Aston Villa’s hopes of progressing to the Champions League knockout rounds were dented as they were beaten 1-0 at Galatasaray.

Unai Emery’s side won their first three games in the league phase but rather than bouncing back from a 3-0 defeat at Barcelona, they suffered another reverse in Istanbul.

Deniz Gul’s 77th minute header was the game’s first shot on target and was enough to seal all three points for the Turkish side.

With games against Paris St Germain and Borussia Dortmund to come either side of Christmas, Unai Emery’s men now have a challenge to finish in the top eight and earn a direct ticket into the knockout phase.

Even more worryingly, this latest loss made for six straight games without a win in all competitions, while Villa failed to register a single shot on target in the 90 minutes. their sixth consecutive defeat

The pre-match talk was about the state of the pitch at RAMS Park, with Galatasaray playing the weekend’s league match away from the stadium in order for the surface to undergo emergency repairs.

As a result, Villa were unable to train on it ahead of the game and the pitch was plied with sand.

But the visitors initially acquitted themselves well and managed the cauldron of noise as they enjoyed a controlled start, with their best moment coming when they made a quick break down the right and the ball ended up with Johan Manzambi, but he could not get a shot away.

Galatasaray came into it as the first half progressed, but did not test Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki, who will have welcomed a quiet opening after his recent troubles.

The intensity increased at the start of the second half and there were two flashpoints as tempers flared.

First, John McGinn and Aleksey Batrakov went into the book after McGinn flew into his counterpart as revenge for a heavy challenge on Alysson by former Tottenham defender Davinson Sanchez.

There was another coming together as Joao Gomes was booked for stopping Yunus Akgun’s counter-attack.

The hosts suddenly had the bit between their teeth and they pushed Villa back, with Aleksey Batrakov flashing a volley well over, before a loose ball from a corner fell to Gul, who showed bravery to head the ball home while taking a kick in the face from Nicolas Jackson.

#920. Xabi Alonso’s and Enzo Maresca’s ‘intensity’ issues prove underrated Mikel Arteta leads our post-Guardiola world

Mikel Arteta is still king in the Premier League, with rivals struggling with intensity

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

‘Intensity’ is the buzzword of the moment, capturing a vibe that is just so Premier League.

For armchair tacticians - in particular for those pundits who lack the capacity for tactical analysis but know they ought to have this sort of thing down - ‘intensity’ is a usefully amorphous concept to deploy; the kind of word you can drop into a list alongside ‘leaving too much space’ and ‘nobody closing down’ and call it punditry.

‘Intensity’ is hard to define because it sits at the cross-section between pressing systems and the psychological. Does a high-intensity midfield press invigorate players to believe in their own mental intensity, or do the players need to feel the intense high-confidence of a high-intensity coach to engage their pressing intensity? It’s almost as if the word has no meaning.

But the application of the word ‘intensity’ across the Premier League weekend just gone can be instructive. Chelsea haven’t got it. Nor do Manchester City. Tottenham Hotspur have it. Liverpool have got it, sometimes, and Arsenal – Arsenal always have it, even if a lot of people don’t want to see it.

If there is a serious tactical point to be made here, it’s about the Premier League as a fast and direct division and - although it might sound sacrilegious to say it – it’s about Pep Guardiola’s modern irrelevance.

The great man himself foresaw this years ago, when he famously mused that “modern football is not positional”, and is instead being defined by “riding the rhythm” like Bournemouth.

Only one of his disciples listened, the one who looks set to win back-to-back Premier League titles. The others are floundering.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Enzo Maresca and Xabi Alonso are both students of Guardiola, the former his assistant at Manchester City and the latter a mentee when playing under Pep at Bayern Munich. Both managers historically prefer very low-tempo possession football (in their title-winning season, Alonso’s Bayer Leverkusen had the slowest direct speed upfield in the Bundesliga, at 1.71 m/s), a hallmark of Guardiola’s suffocating tactical domination of English football across seven years.

But the era of Guardiola ended more than two years ago. Watching Chelsea and Man City play this season, it shows.

Chelsea’s 4-1 defeat to Leeds United followed a pattern of the campaign, in that Alonso’s side appear too soft, steady, and meticulous in their actions to cope with the Premier League’s physicality. Alonso’s rigid ‘positional play’ – demarcated positions, sideways passing, detailed instructions of where each pass should go – is pure Pep. It simply could not cope with Leeds’ man-to-man pressing.

The Premier League is a fast and direct division… the era of Guardiola ended more than two years ago

Leeds recorded more recoveries (51 to 39) and more pressures (508 to 416) than Chelsea, had a considerably lower PPDA (13 to 19) and forced twice as many high turnovers (15 to 7). Yes, Leeds had intensity; Chelsea did not.

Over at the Etihad, it was startling to see the hosts refuse to press Fulham’s defenders at all, instead sitting in a quiet midblock that allowed Alvaro Arbeloa’s side to build momentum. From this low-intensity starting position, City could not engage quickly when Fulham sprung a counter-attack.

Looking at the arc of history, we are currently between eras, perhaps, with Andoni Iraola and Roberto De Zerbi – now there’s intensity – likely to emerge as major players once Long Guardiola fades and “riding the rhythm” takes its place. But in the meantime, Arsenal are in dynasty territory thanks to Mikel Arteta, a Guardiola disciple who cast aside his tutor’s teachings long ago.

He is not given anywhere near enough credit for this.

On Saturday, sloppy mistakes are all that prevented Arsenal from seeing out a brilliantly masterminded victory at St James Park, where Arteta’s tactical instructions pulled the man-to-man Newcastle press out of shape, creating ‘artificial transitions’: build-up attacks that, by baiting a press and then turning it, give the illusion of a counter-attack.

Time and time again, Kai Havertz would pull short as the false nine to drag a centre-back with him, at which point Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke would make clever inverted runs into the space for longer Arsenal passes to hit. It was fast, sharp, and intense – and it led directly to both goals.

It was seriously smart, out-witting Matthias Jaissle’s ‘high-intensity’ football (from the Red Bull school) and proving, again, that Arteta is one of the best tacticians the Premier League has ever seen.

That is not a popular opinion, probably because people do not like the conservatism that has increasingly defined Arsenal’s attacking play, but also because the tactical complexity of what he does – the form of ‘intensity’ his football takes – does not conform to expectations.

Accusations of low intensity are generally a wishy-washy way of saying the plan isn’t working, highlighting a tactical problem without actually defining what it is. But in the cases of Alonso and Maresca, it is easy to diagnose once we watch Arsenal’s verticality, their directness, their urgency in picking apart Newcastle’s game plan.

As usual, Arteta is ahead of the curve, and he comes with a message for Alonso and Maresca: if you want to play with ‘intensity’, you must first let go of the master’s teachings.

Alex Keble is a freelance football journalist based in London, specialising in tactical analysis. He has written for BBC Sport, Goal, The Mirror, The Independent, Football 365, and many others. As well as covering Premier League football, Alex works as a child therapist.

#919. Neuer injury gives Urbig chance to shape Bayern and Germany future

Manuel Neuer's latest injury gives Jonas Urbig a run of games in Bayern's goal. Marc-André ter Stegen remains Germany’s No. 1, but Urbig now has a chance to strengthen his case for the future.

It's no secret that getting playing time is important to the development of any professional footballer – especially if your aspiration is to become the first-choice goalkeeper for your country . For most national team coaches, only a keeper who is playing regularly for his club merits consideration.

Unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception. While he did give Urbig – the backup keeper at Bayern – two starts in his first international break as national team boss, for the upcoming UEFA Nations League matches against Serbia and the Netherlands, Marc-André ter Stegen remains the undisputed No. 1.

But when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich. But this is set to change after Bayern's recent Bundesliga win over Mainz. The 40-year-old Manuel Neuer asked to be subbed off just before halftime, complaining of severe pain in his right foot.

An examination revealed that Neuer has sustained a partial tendon tear in the foot.

"An injury never comes at the right time, but it's part of the game," Neuer wrote on Instagram.

"I've been through this before, and I'll get through this one too. From now on: full focus on recovery. Until then, I will support the boys on the pitch wherever I can."

A partial tendon tear usually results in a layoff of six to 12 weeks, depending on the severity of the injury. Given that Neuer's foot already has some pre-existing damage from previous injuries, his recovery could take even longer.

Although Urbig is now the de-facto first-choice keeper for Bayern, he will still have to bide his time in the national team as understudy to ter Stegen. However, there is a general consensus that someday, Urbig will also become Germany's No. 1. With Neuer's contract running out in the summer, the chance to truly make the Bayern goal his own appears likely in the not-too-distant future.

The match on Saturday was Neuer's 550th in the Bundesliga and he also became the oldest player in a league match in Bayern's history when he took the pitch aged 40 years and 225 days. In other words, he can't go on forever.

One of his most famous predecessors in the Bayern goal has already called on him to draw a line under his highly successful career.

"I would tell him: 'Call it a day, Manu!' You have given an incredible amount to football, you have won everything, and you don't have to prove anything to anyone anymore," Sepp Maier, a member of West Germany's 1974 World Cup winning team told Sport1.

At some point, the now 82-year-old Maier noted, there comes a moment "when your body no longer behaves the way you want it to. And even a Manuel Neuer cannot stave off that moment."

For now, with ter Stegen playing regularly and performing well for Ajax, Germany coach Klopp is under no pressure to make a change. However, the 34-year-old former Barcelona keeper has, like Neuer, become quite injury-prone in recent years. Whenever he's needed, Urbig will be more than happy to seize his opportunity.

#917. Mauricio Pochettino admits Man United’s ‘situation is fragile’ but insists he has a ‘strong team’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Mauricio Pochettino watched his Manchester United side lose 4-0 to Liverpool on Sunday

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino has insisted he has taken over a "strong team" at Manchester United, despite acknowledging that their current predicament is a precarious one.

The Argentine's tenure as head coach began disastrously on Sunday with a heavy 4-0 defeat against rivals Liverpool, leaving them second bottom of the Premier League after 11 fixtures, ahead of only Crystal Palace.

Ahead of Wednesday's Champions League meeting in Lisbon, Sporting boss Paulo Fonseca dismissed the notion that United possess a fragility, and Pochettino pointed to their high-flying finish under Michael Carrick last term as evidence they can reverse their current slump.

"The situation is fragile," Pochettino said. "We are not fragile. We are a strong team, they showed that last season when they finished third and now we are playing in the Champions League.

"Sometimes things happen in football for different reasons. We need to identify why and already we are working on it. I think we are going to turn round the situation.

"We need to go game-by-game. In the end, being at Manchester United is about winning every single game, one is not more important than another.

"We are Manchester United and we need to believe we have the capacity to turn that situation. We are building our identity and that is the most important thing."

United captain Bruno Fernandes agreed that getting back to winning ways is his main focus and only then will the Portuguese midfielder restart talks over signing a new deal.

Fernandes, who joined United from Sporting in January 2020, is into the final year of his contract, which includes an option for another 12 months, although he has turned down two offers of an extension.

Asked what conditions have to be in place to sign a new long-term contract, Fernandes replied: “For us to start winning games and then we can start speaking about contracts. It’s not important now, it’s irrelevant.

“I know it’s my future and I shouldn’t look at it that way because I haven’t got much left in my contract but I’m more worried about getting results, trying to get the club into a position we can be proud of.

“We’ll have time to speak about that. We had conversations, the conversations stopped when that was not as important because the results and performances weren’t at the level they should have been.”

United have won two and lost two in this season’s Champions League, most recently coming from 2-0 behind at Old Trafford to claim a 3-2 win over Roma earlier this month.

Fernandes has played just one knockout tie – against Atletico Madrid in 2022 – during his stint at United.

He added: “When I started my career, I never had the opportunity in the first few years to play Champions League, so that was a faraway dream for me.

“I’m very proud of what I’ve achieved, even if I have only played one time, I still have got many years left in my career, I hope, so I’m going to have many opportunities to do that and why not this season?”

#916. Alonso heckled as Chelsea are humiliated by Leeds

There are two non-negotiables for Chelsea managers. Do not lose at home to Tottenham Hotspur and do not lose at home to Leeds United. But Xabi Alonso has now completed the nightmare double.

Just as Spurs broke their Stamford Bridge hoodoo a few weeks ago, Leeds secured their first win at Chelsea since 1999 by humiliating the hosts after falling a goal behind.

It was 67 long years since Chelsea had last lost at home to Tottenham and Leeds in the same season, and Alonso was left in no doubt about how seriously supporters take that as his team were loudly booed and he was heckled.

Cole Palmer stormed down the tunnel at full time, ignoring the advice of Chelsea’s so-called “cultural architect” Willie Isa to applaud the remaining home fans, and shrugging off the attention of injured striker João Pedro.

Having been left out of the last England squad, Palmer was largely anonymous for Chelsea but he was not alone and Alonso is already facing similar questions to his predecessors about the team’s mentality.

“I felt that probably we are in a fragile moment, mentally,” Alonso said. “When we receive a punch, we didn’t recover that strong, that tough enough and today that was my feeling.

“The fans were disappointed because the expectations from them are high and we feel sorry for them. For sure, it’s not the easiest moment. It’s a fragile moment, but we need to work together and stick together because there is still a long way to go.”

Alonso is yet to name the same starting XI for successive league games and there appears to be no discernible plan or style of play.

Injuries have contributed to Chelsea’s unremarkable start to the season under Alonso – and Moisés Caicedo was forced off early in the first half – but the problems run deeper than the treatment table.

Alonso’s defence has now conceded 20 goals, which has contributed to Chelsea losing five league games already – more than Manchester United. In between three defeats in their last four league games, Chelsea were also knocked out of the Carabao Cup.

The Spaniard had answered questions about Chelsea’s identity, or lack of it, by saying he wanted his team to be competitive. But they were anything but against a Leeds side who had seven more shots than their hosts and five more on target.

It is hard to fathom how, through all the chopping and changing, Wesley Fofana still starts games for Chelsea in defence. It was his pathetic attempted header, which bounced backwards towards his own goal, that contributed to Noah Okafor’s first goal.

Josh Acheampong also got himself into a mess and Okafor was somehow able to squeeze a shot past goalkeeper Emi Martínez despite having three Chelsea players around him.

Chelsea had taken the lead through striker Emmanuel Emegha, on his first start for the club, but from that moment on they were second best with Leeds pair Ethan Ampadu and Ao Tanaka running the middle of the park.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin had hit the crossbar and failed to find the net with three more presentable opportunities in the first half, but he took his chance from the penalty spot eight minutes after the break.

Morgan Rogers had argued that James Justin’s shot hit him too far up his arm for it to be a penalty, but a VAR check upheld referee Michael Oliver’s decision and Calvert-Lewin kept his cool.

That should have been the moment that shook Chelsea into action and prompted a response but, instead, Alonso’s team fell apart and he was unable to provoke a shift in momentum from the touchline.

Just five minutes after Calvert-Lewin had put Leeds ahead, Okafor effectively sealed the victory by firing the ball into the net after Chelsea had failed to deal with a long throw into their penalty area.

Noah Okafor's brace helps seal Leeds' first Premier League win at Stamford Bridge since 1999! 💥 https://t.co/UAmsJziJmZ

“I can’t wait to be on the sofa with coffee and cake and also watch this game back because it was a really good game,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds head coach, said. “I was a bit disappointed even at half-time when it was just a draw, because I think we were the better side from the first to the last.”

John Terry still works with Chelsea’s academy and it might be worth Alonso getting the former captain to speak to the club’s senior players about how to defend and compete. Whatever has been done on the training pitch so far has not worked.

Alonso’s substitutes are yet to register a single goal or assist in the league this season and his changes failed to make any sort of impact here. For the visitors, however, two substitutes combined to score their fourth goal in time added on for stoppages.

Harry Wilson played in Brenden Aaronson and, from a tight angle, he managed to find the back of the net by sending the ball through the legs of Martínez.

The home stands were already half-empty by that point, but some supporters hung around to show their displeasure and Palmer could not contain his anger.

We know what the history of this game is like and what the fans expect - we know they have wanted a win here for a long time. It’s right we can enjoy this performance.

Frank’s start to life at Palace begins with defeat but an improved display. Coventry are up to 13th with their fourth win of the season.

Another home win for Tottenham, who managed the game well and introduced a new star to the Premier League in Williams-Barnett

What a day for Leeds. They scored four and it could have been more. For Chelsea, they lost their way when Caicedo went off and without Joao Pedro, they have lost their spark in attack.

Bournemouth make it nine wins in a row in all competitions after doing enough in the first half to get the job done.

Leeds finish the match in style as Aaronson puts the seal on an impressive away day.

It’s all over and Sunderland deservedly leave with a point. Villa will be very disappointed by their display.

What was I saying in the last post?! The home side are on the attack Thomas-Asante pokes a shot at goal and forces Henderson into a save but hits his own player McNeil, who bundles the ball in the net.

Can Chelsea stage a late fightback? Will we get a winner between Coventry and Palace?

Needing a goal, Emery makes a bold decision to take off Villa’s top scorer and bring on Madjo.

Despite the two-goal lead and the magnificent debut performance of Luca Williams-Barnett, the home support has remained subdued throughout the afternoon.

At times, the shouts of two children sat just behind the press box feel like by far the loudest noise in the stadium - although that might just be proximity.

Much quieter half at the CBS Arena but Palace are more likely to get a third goal.

This has gone from bad to worse for Chelsea. One supporter near the dug-outs was so angry at Leeds scoring a third goal that he got up and screamed his displeasure at manager Xabi Alonso.

1999 was the last time Leeds won at Chelsea. Today looks like they will get another, as Okafor takes advantage of more poor defending to finish past Martinez.

Villa’s fans are now chanting loudly for substitute John McGinn to be introduced.

They are getting their wish, too, as the Scotland international is coming on with winger Ibrahim Mbaye.

Morgan Rogers and Chelsea are pretty upset about that penalty being awarded to Leeds. They felt the ball struck him too far up his arm to be a penalty. Calvert-Lewin took his spot-kick superbly and it’s gone very, very quiet among the home fans.

Everything Luca Williams-Barnett touches is turning to gold today. He has a goal to his name already, and adds an assist just six minutes into the second half.

From almost the halfway line, he drove forward, weaving his way expertly into the box before picking out Dominic Solanke in the middle of the box, who tapped the ball into the back of the net.

However, the atmosphere is still a touch subdued, despite James Maddison urging the crowd to make themselves heard almost immediately after the goal, the noise drops to almost a murmur.

Rogers blocks Bogle’s drive with his arm and Michael Oliver gives a penalty to Leeds. After a long check, VAR confirms it.

Calvert-Lewin steps up and sends Martinez the wrong way. The away team deserves this. They have been the better side. That is Calvert-Lewin’s 100th club career goal.

Williams-Barnet gets one-on-one with Furlong and gets past him with ease before firing a cross for Solanke to finish.

The whistle blows for the second half around the grounds. What will the second 45 minutes have for us?

A real lack of quality here from both teams, and Sunderland deserve credit for weathering the early pressure.

Villa appear short of creativity and have managed only one shot on target in the first-half.

Sunderland have defended resolutely and caused Villa’s back-four some problems in the rare moments they have attacked.

Unai Emery marched into the dressing room after the half-time whistle and has much to ponder.

Some boos from the Chelsea fans at half-time. Calvert-Lewin could have had a hat-trick in that first half, sending one header against the bar, two too close to Martinez and flicking a shot just wide. Leeds also had a goal ruled out for offside.

Chelsea just stopped playing after taking the lead.

That half was all about Luca Williams-Barnett. The 18-year-old scored in his first start, and had two opportunities to add to his tally just before the break. He had a header tipped over the bar by Christian Walton and a chance from close range stopped on the line. The future looks bright, as they say.

However, Tottenham faded after a strong opening 15 minutes, and Ipswich were able to break up play and get forward more, exploiting the home side’s lack of a defensive midfielder, and that will be something for Roberto De Zerbi to address in the break.

We have whistles around the ground. That was breathless stuff.

The visitors will feel they should be in front at the break. First, Muharemovic thinks he has scored when he head in a cross from Justin but he was offside.

Then Ampadu’s long throw finds Calvert-Lewin in space and his shot is saved by Martinez. Should have done better there.

Bournemouth finish the half in style. Kluivert gets the second when he taps in a cross from Tavernier.

Palace hit back again. Pino clips a cross to Larsen at the far post and he heads past Rushworth coolly.

Courtesy of Opta: Aged 18 years and 51 days, Luca Williams-Barnett is Tottenham Hotspur’s youngest Premier League goalscorer since Gareth Bale against Fulham in September 2007 (18y 47d).

Villa are in desperate need of a spark and one has to wonder when John McGinn will be introduced. McGinn is on the bench today and the home team are crying out for some inspiration.

Villa did start brilliantly, yet the game has now petered out into a mess of misplaced passes and poor decision-making.

Still no clean sheet for Emi Martinez. But Noah Okafor’s goal wasn’t his fault – he was let down by some bad defending from Wesley Fofana and Josh Acheampong.

Martinez did start Chelsea’s 2-0 victory over Everton, but he didn’t last the full game as he had to be replaced because of injury.

A touch of Hollywood royalty in attendance at Tottenham on this cold November afternoon with Sir Kenneth Branagh and Ryan Reynolds in attendance.

Reynolds is a co-owner of Wrexham, who are currently playing in the Championship at Lincoln City, but he has chosen to watch football in north London instead.

Sakamoto puts Palace back in front with a brilliant finish. Rudoni gets away from Khalaili and crosses to the Japan international. Sakamoto brings it down nicely then rifles a shot into the top corner.

That lead did not last long for Chelsea. The away side hit back within three minutes as Okafor shoots through the legs of Colwill and into the net.

Another full debutant and another goal. This time at Stamford Bridge as Emegha latches onto a ball from Rogers and blasts an unstoppable shot from distance.

Emegha had to wait a while to make his first start for Chelsea, but he’s marked it with a really well taken goal. Leeds will be disappointed with the time and space he and Morgan Rogers, who provided the assist, were given, but it was a good finish.

Caicedo just can’t get going this season. That back injury that forced him off the pitch for a minute earlier has now resulted in him having to be replaced by Jordan Henderson. That’s a real blow to Alonso and Chelsea.

Villa were completely dominant in the opening ten minutes but Sunderland have now managed to subdue the home team.

Johan Manzambi and Nicolas Jackson are both impressing for the home team. Villa do appear a little vulnerable in defence when Sunderland do break forward.

Today will be a day that 18-year-old Luca Williams-Barnett will not forget in a hurry, he has been energetic since the start and marked his maiden Premier League start with an early goal.

The actual goal might have been a tap-in, but it has injected life into the crowd who had otherwise been largely subdued from the start.

Confusion on the touchline for Chelsea. Caicedo was down after hurting his back. Alonso tried to stop his phyisos going straight on to the pitch, but referee Michael Oliver called them on. That meant Caicedo had to spend a minute off the pitch under the latest rules.

Remember this moment because on his first senior start Williams-Barnet has made it a special one with goal. It was scrappy but he will not care. The Tottenham fans have been talking about his young fan for a long time.

Equaliser for Palace and Frank. Very good response from his players as Larsen flicks the ball to Pino and the Spain international fires into the net.

No shots on target from either side but it is already shaping up to be attack vs defence. Villa are dominating the goal and looking threatening.

Awoniyi is through one-on-one with Henderson, goes around the keeper but Disasi does brilliantly to recover and make the block.

Worst possible start for Frank and Palace as Awoniyi gets his second goal of the season with a cool finish.

A video of De Zerbi saying “let’s go” in a manner that might be more at home in American Football is shown before the teams come out onto the pitch.

The atmosphere feels a bit subdued so far, but it is an important match for Tottenham.

This is probably the kiss of death from me, but I’m really looking forward to watching Tarik Muharemovic today. The defender has impressed me every time I’ve watched Leeds on television this season and looks to be one of the signings of the summer. Dare I say it, but Chelsea could have done worse than sign him given their troubles at the back. Emi Martinez is back in goal for the home side. He’s yet to keep a clean sheet since signing from Aston Villa.

Aston Villa: Suzuki, Wan-Bissaka, Harwood-Bellis, Torres, Maatsen, Kamara, Goretzka, Alysson, Manzambi, Buendia, Jackson.Subs: Bizot, Mings, Barkley, McGinn, Mbaye, Joao Gomes, Madjo, Cisse, Hemmings.

Thomas Frank declared “it’s good to be back in the circus” of football management ahead of his first match as Crystal Palace boss.

The 53-year-old Dane admitted he could have easily spent a few more months sipping wine, “eating too well” and collecting passport stamps, but something resonated when he asked his wife why he was tempted to seek out a new job and she told him, “(It’s) because you can’t help yourself”.

Frank hinted that there was more behind the story to his disappointing spell at Tottenham he might one day reveal, but for now he has a team to rescue from a relegation fight, beginning with today’s trip to Coventry.

If you don’t learn from any of your jobs, I don’t think you reflect, I don’t think you improve, and I don’t think you get better.

Of course there’s a lot of things I have been reflecting over. The details, that will be for another time, but I can say I’ve learned, definitely.

I was very aware I didn’t want to do anything in the summer. I put a statement out there, I needed more time. I can actually, honestly say I would have been fine if it was three, four, five, six, seven months more, because it’s good to be back in the circus, but it’s also unbelievably good not to be in, especially if you enjoy life, which I do.

I was spending time with family and friends and doing all that, but I think the club, the way Palace is, how well Steve Parish especially spoke about the club and ideas, Matt Hobbs and Iain Moody and these guys, too, helped convince me it was a good idea.

Construction news: work on the North Stand behind one of the Villa Park goals continues to progress.

There are clear structural changes since Villa’s last home game and a mural of fans makes it more appealing to look at.

This stand is scheduled to be ready for next season and will increase Villa’s capacity to over 50,000.

Tottenham’s impressive run of form came to a crashing halt with a 1-0 defeat to Leeds just before the international break, but manager Roberto De Zerbi will be hoping for a fresh start - even if he will not be pitchside after picking up a second yellow card of the season.

De Zerbi made six changes from the aforementioned defeat to Leeds, including a first start for teenager Luca Williams-Barnett, a player who has come through the club’s academy.

There is no place in the squad for Sandro Tonali or Tosin Adarabioyo, but James Maddison will start for the first time since the 2-0 defeat to Chelsea in October.

Aston Villa 2.0 was always likely to be a slow-burner, and it is proving exactly that for Unai Emery.

His team has impressed and underwhelmed in equal measure so far this season but this is an opportunity to hoist themselves up the table.

A clean sheet would be a good starting point, as they have not secured a shutout in front of their own fans in the league since March.

There is no Alejandro Garnacho or Tammy Abraham in the matchday squad today.

Good afternoon and welcome to coverage from the Premier League as domestic football returns after an international break.

We have five matches to bring you, including Chelsea vs Leeds, Aston Villa vs Sunderland and Tottenham vs Ipswich.

Xabi Alonso said his Chelsea side needs to learn to deal with the absence of Joao Pedro as the Blues struggle for goals in the absence of their injured striker.

The Brazilian has not played since the 2-0 win over Everton on October 17 and will be unavailable again today.

Without a focal point in the number nine position, Chelsea’s goal output has been dramatically reduced and they have dropped to fifth and having suffered two defeats in their last three games.

“(We need) the whole team for that,” said Alonso. “It’s not just the strikers that can score. We can score from set-pieces, from defenders, from midfielders.

“It’s teamwork. For sure Joao is an important player but we need to deal with this time without him. So far we have tried different options and we need to keep trying.

“We need to deal with it. It’s not that I’m going to look for one explanation. I think that there are more explanations for one defeat than missing just one player.”

Tottenham will not have their manager, Roberto De Zerbi, on the touchline after receiving three yellow cards this season.

Gary O’Neil is targeting a “special” result at Tottenham, but promised Ipswich will not make any drastic changes after a four-match winless run.

Ipswich lost 2-1 at home to Bournemouth before the two-week break, which followed draws with Hull and Nottingham Forest along with a narrow defeat at Manchester City, but O’Neil is happy with his new-look group.

“There won’t be any drastic changes. The odd personnel change, (but) I don’t think it’s going to be a big shift for us,” O’Neil told a press conference.

“It’s a very well-balanced squad. There’s going to be no massive uplifts or downgrades when we have to change players within this group.”

Aston Villa will have Johan Manzambi available for the visit of Sunderland.

The midfielder did not feature for Switzerland during the recent international break because of a calf injury but he has trained with the rest of the squad and can feature today.

Villa can also call on right-back Aaron Wan-Bissaka after a muscle injury ruled him out for six matches. His return is timely as Matty Cash is unavailable.

Cash was suspended for Villa’s 4-4 draw with Manchester United before the international break but suffered a concussion while away with Poland.

#915. Arsenal v Borussia Dortmund LIVE: Gunners held to draw but remain unbeaten in Champions League

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Arsenal 1-1 Borussia Dortmund: The Gunners remain unbeaten in the Champions League but failed to capitalise at the Emirates

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Arsenal were held to a 1-1 draw in their Champions League clash against Borussia Dortmund but remain on course to qualify in one of the automatic knockout spots.

The Gunners started the clash at the Emirates Stadium in quick fashion and controlled possession with short, slick passes and forward runs. Noni Madueke impressed on the right and set up Viktor Gyokeres to score the opening goal from outside the penalty area.

However, Mikel Arteta’s team slackened off in discipline as the half went on which allowed Dortmund to gain a foothold. The Bundesliga leaders then came out from half-time with renewed vigour and secured an equaliser through Maximilian Beier.

With the scores level both teams created further chances, Declan Rice hit the post and Jobe Bellingham had a goal disallowed, but neither could find the back of the net again.

The points were shared leaving Arsenal fifth in the league phase table with Dortmund one point below them in seventh.

Relive the updates from Arsenal v Borussia Dortmund, below:

It isn’t yet a real problem for Arsenal, but it may just breathe a bit of life into the number of teams looking up at them: a sudden inability to kill games.

And while that usually refers to finishing - in the sense of scoring - it is here as applicable to their ability to strangle matches.

"That's what we want [to finish in the top eight],” Arteta told Amazon Prime Video.

“We have a big game against Manchester City at home on Sunday so we need to recover really well, we have four days to do that and sustain that momentum the way we are playing and the win will come."

The Arsenal manager also spoke about Noni Madueke and his reaction to the result in the dressing room.

Arteta revealed: "He [Madueke] was really good but you go in the dressing room and he is not satisfied because we had so many chances where we can put the ball in the net and finish the action."

Of his Swedish striker, Mikel Arteta added: "He was great, not only the goal but he connected with the team.

“We found him in various ways in many situations and it was always a threat."

The Arsenal manager said: "The performance was superb and there is no question about that from the start to the end.

“We played against a really good side and the domination and threat was really impressive. The general feeling inside the dressing room is that we should reward ourselves with more.

"I love the courage, the fluidity and the understanding with the players with and without the ball.”

“We are very confident. We will go for it."

Arsenal’s goalscorer Viktor Gyokeres spoke after the game.

He said: "We could have scored in the second half. We could have won the game in many different ways.

“We played well and created a lot of chances, we deserved to win the game but sometimes it is like that.

"The most important thing is that we create those chances and get shots on goal. For sure we will score goals when games are coming up."

Manchester City were also held to a draw tonight as they finished their encounter with Napoli 2-2.

Meanwhile, Jude Bellingham scored a screamer in a 5-1 victory for Real Madrid over PSV Eindhoven.

Arsenal try their best to secure an equaliser but it’s not enough and the points are shared at the Emirates Stadium.

90 mins: Four minutes of added time to play.

#914. Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?

Hitler once called Eastern Europe "Germany's India." A new exhibition examines the links between colonialism and Nazism, and the bitter debate over where comparisons illuminate history and where they fall short.

Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men."

But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared remains the subject of intense debate.

This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust. Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history.

"I do think this is nonsense," says Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposedly be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story.

The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers. The juxtaposition highlights the contrast between colonial violence and the industrialized mass murder of the Holocaust.

Yet it also points to connections: Whips were used in Nazi concentration camps, while Fascist Italy deployed chemical weapons against civilians and soldiers during its invasion of Ethiopia (then Abyssinia) in 1935-36.

In the 1930s, anti-colonial thinkers from India to the Caribbean argued that colonialism and fascism were two sides of the same coin. "There is nothing new or original about the blustering exploits of Hitler and Mussolini," observed the Trinidadian journalist and Pan-Africanist George Padmore in 1938. "They have all been used before by the British in their efforts to obtain the subjection of less powerfully armed and more industrially backward people."

European colonial rule was marked by the ruthless exploitation of people and resources, often enforced through extreme violence. In "The Origins of Totalitarianism" (1951), German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt argued that colonial territories served as laboratories for racial ideologies and practices of domination that could be applied beyond the legal constraints of Europe. Arendt described how these later "boomeranged" back into Europe and helped shape totalitarian politics in distinct and unprecedented form.

The Congo Free State, King Leopold II of Belgium's private colony from 1885 to 1908, became notorious for its extreme brutality, as colonial authorities used executions, amputations and sexual violence to ensure rubber production quotas were met.

Forced labor was also central to Nazi rule, with millions of Poles, Ukrainians, Russians and others from the Soviet Union, and Jews, subjected to exploitation and "Vernichtung durch Arbeit" ("extermination through work"). Within a few years, the regime mobilized around 13 to 14 million forced laborers, a scale comparable to the transatlantic slave trade over more than three centuries. The Nazis sought to extract value from their victims at every stage, confiscating their property, exploiting their labor, and even harvesting gold teeth and hair from the dead.

While racism underpinned both colonial empires and Nazism, Malinowski says the goals were different. The colonial powers tended to present assimilation as a path to advancement, forcing colonized people to adopt European culture, serve imperial interests, and suggesting that a select, educated few could gain opportunities, for example at elite institutions such as Oxford or Cambridge. "This is definitely not something that the Nazi regime is offering to Poles or to Russians or let alone to Jews," added Malinowski.

"In terms of violence, colonial violence was just as extreme as Nazi violence. But Nazi violence was annihilatory and exterminatory compared to colonial violence in the colonies," says Edward Kissi, a historian at the School of Interdisciplinary Global Studies at the University of South Florida. He points to the example of how, unlike European colonial powers in Africa, the Nazis pursued the elimination of Black-Germans or peoples of African descent in Germany through forced sterilization. "Even in racism, colonial color-based racism and colonial anti-Jewish sentiments were fundamentally different from what the Nazis pursued."

On October 2, 1904, German General Lothar von Trotha issued the "Vernichtungsbefehl" ("extermination order") following the Herero uprising in German South West Africa (present-day Namibia). Historians generally attribute the order to a combination of racial ideology, a desire to terrorize the population into submission, and efforts to secure colonial control over land, labor and resources. Between 1904 and 1908, an estimated 60,000 to 80,000 Herero (around 80% of the population) and 10,000 (around half the population) Nama died.

One area where the exhibition draws no direct parallel is the industrialized killing carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau. "Where the two things really diverge is the Holocaust and is the systematic mass murder of the European Jews and it's murder for the very purpose of murder," explains Malinowski. The deportation of around 1,800 Jews from the Greek islands of Rhodes and Kos in July 1944 illustrates how Nazi persecution often defied military or economic logic. Even after the war was effectively lost, the community was transported to Auschwitz, where most were murdered immediately upon arrival.

The issue of the "singularity" of the Holocaust came to the fore during the 1980s "Historikerstreit" ("historians' dispute"). Historian Ernst Nolte argued that Nazism should be understood in the wider context of 20th-century political violence, and as a response to Bolshevik terror in particular. Critics accused him of downplaying German responsibility for Nazi crimes.

Since 2020, a renewed debate dubbed the "Historikerstreit 2.0" has focused on whether the Holocaust should be viewed as a unique reference point in German memory culture or be understood alongside the histories of colonialism, racism and empire. The dispute now is less about the legitimacy of comparison than about its implications.

The mass murder of tens of thousands of the Herero and Nama during four years of German colonial rule is now regarded as the first genocide of the 20th-century. But in 2016, Nama representatives walked out of talks after Germany's chief negotiator said what happened was "incomparable" to the Holocaust. The German government has since recognized the events as genocide "from today's perspective," but it has not yet accepted legal liability or agreed to pay formal reparations.

Martinican intellectual Aime Cesaire argued in "Discourse on Colonialism" (1950) that Europe condemned under Nazism forms of violence it had long accepted in its colonies. More than 70 years later, the exhibition opens amid renewed debates over the definition of settler colonialism and genocide, and the meaning of "never again," sharpened by Nicaragua's case against Germany at the International Court of Justice over Germany's support for Israel during the war in Gaza and its alleged failure to uphold its obligations under the Genocide Convention to prevent genocide.

These tensions are reflected in visitors' comments in the exhibition's epilogue, even though the exhibition itself does not address Israel or Palestine beyond a reference to Mohammed Amin al-Husseini, appointed Grand Mufti of Jerusalem in 1921.

Germany has unequivocally accepted responsibility for the Holocaust, which is front and center of the country's culture of remembrance.  However, Kissi likens Germany's apparent reluctance to reckon with its colonial history to debates in the US over slavery, in Cambodia over the Khmer Rouge, and in Turkey over the Armenian genocide. According to him, Germany's contemporary identity cannot be fully understood without examining its colonial history and the ways the Nazis appropriated and transformed aspects of that legacy.

"I think Germans and all other human beings who have experienced violent pasts and difficult pasts should be very careful not to delink or dissociate those facts from their present," Kissi said. "These are historical patterns. It is better to deal with these historical patterns and discomforts than to just fight them and then say this has absolutely nothing to do with German national identity."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence" is on show at the German Historical Museum until April 11, 2027.

Willian had a long wait to get his move to Chelsea in 2013 and kept crossing paths with them along the way

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Willian has revealed how Chelsea tried to sign him months before he scored twice against them in the Champions League – and recalled the eyebrow-raising gift he received from a Blues supporter after the game.

The Brazilian winger joined Shakhtar Donetsk from Corinthians in 2007, aged just 19, but admits that he initially had reservations about moving to Ukraine.

Five years later, Chelsea were attempting to bring him to Stamford Bridge. Their January 2012 bid was rejected - but Willian went on to compel them to try again by scoring twice against the Blues in a dramatic 3-2 Champions League defeat that November.

Willian told FourFourTwo: "It wasn't easy. At that time, going straight to Ukraine was not my main goal. I think that every player, especially at that time, who dreamed of going to Europe, wanted to go to Italy or Spain."

"When this offer from Shakhtar came, my family and I talked about it and thought long and hard about whether to accept it. At first, we refused.

"But they kept insisting that I should at least go there to visit the club, visit the city, and learn more about their project. I ended up agreeing."

"I spent a few days there, and I liked what I saw, including the club's structure. There were already other Brazilians playing there too. That certainly made it easier for me to accept the offer.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I remember that months before that game, Chelsea had already made an offer for me.

"he game was in November and their offer came in January 2012 - but Shakhtar didn't want to let me go."

"So, in the end, I stayed at Shakhtar and kept trying to leave. Then, in the group stage, I ended up scoring two goals at Stamford Bridge, so it was special.

"There's something funny about that day: after the match, a fan gave me a Chelsea shirt with my name on it and a question mark in place of the number. As if to say, 'what number will he wear when he plays here?'

"I thought it was funny and even took a photo holding that shirt!"

That supporter would eventually get their wish, in a roundabout way: Willian left Shakhtar for Anzhi Makhachkala in January 2013 before finally completing his move to Chelsea that August.

#911. Missed chances resurface old concerns for Mikel Arteta and Arsenal

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Arsenal 1-1 Borussia Dortmund: The Gunners had to settle for a draw against the Bundesliga leaders after their forward line failed to close out the Champions League tie at the Emirates

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

It isn’t yet a real problem for Arsenal, but it may just breathe a bit of life into the number of teams looking up at them: a sudden inability to kill games.

And while that usually refers to finishing - in the sense of scoring - it is here as applicable to their ability to strangle matches.

Because, for the second match in two, and third in eight, Arsenal have allowed a lead to fritter away and a seemingly cast-iron win to become a frustrating draw, this time at home to Borussia Dortmund. That shouldn't be cause for huge alarm given they are the Bundesliga leaders, and a very good side up against an Arsenal team with changes. Mikel Arteta's team were also generally excellent, which he did praise them for.

Viktor Gyokeres’ brilliant opening goal wasn’t enough. Gyokeres himself may not be enough, but more aggravating for Mikel Arteta here was how their backline was just opened for Maximilian Beier’s equaliser and countless other earlier chances.

So, a previously formidable place in the Champions League top eight becomes that bit more fragile, in the same way the Premier League lead isn’t what it could have been.

This latest example immediately follows that 2-2 draw at Newcastle United, having also happened in their last Champions League game against German opposition: another 2-2 at Bayern Munich.

That fixture obviously carries a different expectation, but it’s still the same issue. It’s now happened three times in eight games, creating an unusual angst around a team that had previously been playing with the assurance of champions.

And that is the greater quandary for Arteta, at least until January.

It’s long been discussed that this attack isn’t as strong or as deep as it should be, and that Arsenal will look at left-sided forward options in January.

That isn’t really a problem if Arsenal don’t concede, as had been the case for most of this campaign. Before Newcastle, they’d only conceded in three league games, even if one of those was a 3-0 beating to Brighton.

Generally, though, the old 1-0 to the Arsenal had become a death sentence for the opposition.

If they went ahead, you didn’t get in behind. Not so much lately.

Even this match, if admittedly with half the team changed, saw Borussia Dortmund repeatedly get at them through the centre. That was the source of Maximilian Beier’s tidy equaliser, and elements of it had similarities to Harvey Barnes’ equaliser on Saturday.

Arteta, after seeing his team concede three goals in two games, will now be fixated on tightening up.

There, it was perhaps some surprise that he didn’t give William Saliba minutes. Ezri Konsa doesn’t exactly deserve to lose his place, though, and it was Gabriel turned for the equaliser anyway.

Either way, their usual machine of a defensive structure isn’t as well calibrated right now, and that then puts a focus on that forward line.

It has been the lingering doubt over a season that looks set to have little substantial title challenge, and offers a strikingly good chance for the club to retain the title for the first time since the 1930s.

Is it at all possible that they just fail to score enough that games that should become wins instead become draws, doubt is created and others are allowed back in?

Gyokeres, as ever, almost encapsulated this: a forward that has qualities but not enough to really be the starter.

When given space to shoot in the first half, he emphatically showed that quality. When required to score in a more pressured situation, he missed the chance of the game.

This is just another frustration for Arteta. Despite again giving up a lead, they had more than enough chances to reclaim it. Gyokeres wasn’t the only attacker culpable. Noni Madueke, recently on such fine form, passed up a brilliant chance just before half-time. Arsenal generally just looked rushed rather than ruthless.

That decisiveness just wasn’t there, though.

Many might say Bukayo Saka wasn’t there, but Arteta has most of his options back. If he is really serious about winning this Champions League, in the way he dreams, Arsenal surely go back into the market in January.

It isn’t the only question for Arteta right now, though. He needs his defence tightened.

He needs his team to recover that recent assurance.

This isn’t yet a real problem, after all. It’s just a recent one, which suggests it might weigh over them for the next spell.

And next up in the league are Manchester City, in that home fixture freighted with so much narrative.

Next up in the Champions League are Real Madrid, who don’t even need Vinicius Junior to show their killer instinct. They’ve got it almost everywhere in attack.

Arsenal had a look in the summer, but now need to look elsewhere - as well as within the team.

#910. Whiff of arrogance as Arsenal unexpectedly implode

Arsenal were cruising. This was life on Premier League easy street, but from complete control of this game against Newcastle United, they tossed it away. It was a spectacular, unexpected implosion. They were extremely fortunate to escape with a point.

You cannot switch off away from home in the Premier League and you certainly can never be complacent against a team with Newcastle’s home crowd behind them.

From control to disarray. From looking like champions, Arsenal, who also lost goalkeeper David Raya to a worrying looking injury, rumbled under pressure. To go from dominance to being grateful for a draw, this was a flaky side of the Premier League leaders we have not seen for a while.

“We have lost two points,” said manager Mikel Arteta. “We were exceptional in the first half, the intensity and the quality, we should have been two, three or four goals up.

“When you don’t do that, in the second half you cannot give the opposition belief and you cannot give them goals. We did both. We started to lose duels, second balls, we gave it away.”

Was it arrogance? Did the title-holders start to believe they were simply too good to be hurt or worried by a team with Newcastle’s obvious limitations? It looked like it. The way Arsenal fell apart as soon as the momentum in the game shifted in the home team’s favour in the second half was shocking.

Newcastle were dreadful before the break and managed just one attack before half-time. Perhaps it was all too easy for Arteta’s side.
